entry.title: Re: ATC Table Attributes Check: six things I learned reading the code (and running it on two systems
entry.content:
@Atul_Joshi85 thank you, and sorry for the late reply. Governance was the question I had in my head after writing this: if a team decides to really use this check as a gate, how much noise will it create?

So today I counted it in my S/4HANA 2023 lab, from the technical settings of the 296 custom transparent tables. Only 2 have log changes on with data class APPL0, which is the 0022 error, priority 1. Only 1 is a small table with buffering allowed but switched off, the 0003 warning. And 5 customizing tables (delivery class C) still have buffering not allowed, the 0010 case.

What surprised me was the other side: only 2 of the 296 tables have buffering switched on at all. Almost all of them are application tables (delivery class A), and 0010 doesn't look at those.

So for me the check is much quieter than its reputation. I would block the release on its priority 1 and 2 findings, because they are few and each one is a real decision, and go through the information messages once, table by table, instead of exempting them all.

I counted the settings, I didn't run ATC on all 296 tables. If you have a number from a bigger system, I would like to see it.

entry.title: Closing the Workforce Plan-to-Execution Gap with SAP Business AI Platform
entry.content:
While the upcoming AI transformation is driving conversations around task-based organisational redesign and skill-based operating models, the reality is that most organisations have yet to achieve a systematic approach to workforce development aligned with their business strategy and financial plan.    

These organisations can accurately route millions of supply chain shipments, manufacture complex hardware with millimeter precision, and micro-segment their customer base in granular detail. Yet, when asked for a clear, forward-looking projection of their workforce capabilities and cost trajectory, they hit a wall—falling back on cumbersome manual alignment processes and disconnected spreadsheets. 

The consequences are familiar: the notorious Q4 hiring freeze triggered by unexpected cost overruns, or periodic waves of restructuring and layoffs that seem increasingly common in an unpredictable business environment.   

In my opinion, this disconnect stems from at least three systemic challenges:

  • Business and Workforce Strategy are out of sync: There is no systematic connection between where the business is heading and what this means for the development of the workforce. With systematic I mean, yes, there might be presentations and high level alignment but this rarely translates to the operational reality. Business strategy and realities often evolve very fast, while workforce strategies remain static, creating expensive capability mismatches and misaligned headcount growth.
  • Finance and Workforce Data are disconnected: Headcount figures in HR often follow a different logic than then way Finance is looking at the supposedly same data, often leading to conflicting numbers or even a lack at reporting HR and Finance data in a common structure.
  • Workforce Plans do not translate into Operations: Even when a solid workforce strategy exists, it often sits on a shelf in the corporate strategy ivory tower. It rarely reaches the operational hiring desk where day-to-day talent acquisition decisions actually take place.

To develop the workforce in lockstep with the business is first and foremost a top management responsibility. eFrom my perspective, unless strategic workforce management is an explicit board priority, initiatives will fail—not from a lack of tooling or processes, but simply due to a lack of governance and the discipline to adhere to the plan. It must become deeply embedded in how the enterprise is run, operating as an end-to-end, closed-loop management discipline:  Assess, Plan, Execute, Monitor and Adjust. 

The following article outlines a pragmatic approach to aligning your workforce with financial plans and business strategy. While core principles apply broadly, organizations will naturally adapt the details to their specific business context and industry dynamics.

The visual below maps this journey across eight concrete steps, highlighting both the business focus and the supporting technology:

 

Let’s explore how each step works in practice.

Step 1: Align Workforce Data to Business Terms

Business Context

To get to a broadly accepted view of the workforce, business leaders and HR must speak the same language. From my experience it is very difficult to have a meaningful conversation about the workforce if data gets presented in granular HR taxonomies that are not reflecting the language of the business. If your job architecture contains thousands of hyper-granular job codes and an incomprehensible skills taxonomy, business leaders tune out and a constructive dialog is not happening.

Key Questions

  • Are your HR job architectures too granular and complex for business leaders to engage with?
  • Do you have a clear strategic categorization (e.g., core, transformation, non-core) to prioritize capabilities along business priorities?
  • Are your office locations categorized by strategic value and cost tiers?
  • Can you easily distinguish between individual contributors and people managers across combined job grades?

Conceptual Approach

Add a layer of planning clusters on top of your HR data to simplify complex data structures and align language with the business:

  • Role Clustering: Consolidate disparate niche titles into role clusters (e.g., mapping multiple Sales roles into "Quota Carriers").
  • Strategic Segmentation: Classify capabilities into clear priority horizons (growth, stable, or declining).
  • Location Tiers: Group regional offices into cost and strategic value archetypes.
  • Seniority Banding: Cluster different job grades into overarching seniority levels to simplify career hierarchy tracking.
  • Role Type Differentiation: Differentiate between individual contributors and people managers across combined job grades.

The SAP Business AI Platform Solution

By leveraging LLMs on SAP Generative AI Hub, organizations can automatically analyze thousands of job titles and descriptions to map them into clear, high-level role clusters. The same can be performed on dimensions like location, clustering for example by cost or talent availability. A lightweight app created with Joule Studio enables HR and Business to jointly perform this exercise. Once defined, these clusters are saved directly in SAP Business Data Cloud's semantic layer, making them instantly available for reuse across all workforce planning models and analytical reports.

 

Step 2: Assess the Current Workforce Composition

Business Context

Any viable planning starts by understanding the current as-is situation. Getting a good understanding requires looking at the workforce simultaneously through at least three lenses: workforce composition, capability, and financial cost. Whereas most organizations have some form of workforce dashboard, it is typcically the bridge to financial cost which prevent a full picture.

Key Questions

  • How is our workforce structured today?
  • What is our total workforce spending, and how much of it goes to full-time employees versus contractors?
  • Is our personnel spending growing faster than our business revenue and operational output?
  • Which core skills exist in our teams today, and where do we have critical capability gaps?

Conceptual Approach

Give leaders clear, direct access to workforce composition and cost data ideally for the total (internal and external) workforce. Replacing scattered spreadsheets with a shared source of truth keeps discussions focused on strategic alignment and decisions rather than debating whose numbers are right.

The SAP Business AI Platform Solution

People Intelligence in SAP Business Data Cloud provides ready to use insights based SAP SuccessFactors data, eliminating manual exports and data cleanup. Business and HR leaders can get a joint understanding of their workforce via SAP Analytics Cloud Dashboards and even use natural language to generate insights with SAP Joule. The SAP Business Data Cloud also facilitates joining People and Finance Data on one central platform either via Data Products or custom data integration.

 

Step 3: Analyze External Talent Market Trends

Business Context

Looking only at your internal headcount misses key context from the broader talent market. When shaping a target workforce model, external market trends show what skills are available, where hiring competition is rising, and what capabilities are becoming critical across your industry. In my opinion, external benchmarks are what management is very interested in to inform target setting. Questions like what our top competitors are doing and what their workforce looks like ground discussions around industry best practices.

Another hot topic is understanding where AI can be leveraged to create workforce efficiencies, allowing you to redirect investment toward strategic growth areas. Many vendors are offering this kind of analysis now. Shortly after the "ChatGPT moment," I experimented with this approach myself—I believe it remains just as relevant today, and you can learn more about it in a previous blog post.

Key Questions

  • Which jobs and profiles are experiencing the highest market demand in the industry?
  • What emerging skills and roles are defining our industry over the next 3–5 years?
  • What does the workforce composition of key competitors look like, and in which locations are they expanding?
  • Where are critical skills becoming too scarce or cost-prohibitive to buy externally?
  • Which roles have high potential for automation or AI augmentation?

Conceptual Approach

Connect external market data providers directly to your internal workforce data. Mapping market benchmarks directly to your internal roles gives leaders continuous visibility into talent availability, wage shifts, and skill demand instead of relying on one-off research projects.

The SAP Business AI Platform Solution

SAP Business Data Cloud offers data integration with external sources, supported by zero-copy sharing with platforms like Databricks, Snowflake, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Fabric. Additionally, specialized market intelligence vendors can be queried directly via standard integration protocols, allowing Joule to bring real-time talent benchmarks right into your planning workflow. SAP Generative AI Hub also helps automatically map internal and external data structures—such as job families and skill taxonomies—to keep everything consistent.

 

Step 4: Forecast Attrition and Retirement

Business Context

To build a realistic plan for your future workforce, you need to understand how natural turnover and retirement patterns will shape your headcount over time. This baseline directly determines how much external hiring is truly required to reach your target state. Just as importantly, it highlights the natural wiggle room you have to proactively reshape your workforce without resorting to unexpected restructuring or layoffs.
In the past, I have often encountered the perception that the workforce is too static to change meaningfully, and restructuring is inherently hard and painful. This is where this wiggle room—what I like to call "Transformation Potential" generated by natural attrition—comes in handy. It allows you to develop the organization toward the desired target state without disruptive reorganizations. When used systematically, this alone can sometimes be enough to bring workforce evolution fully in line with future business strategy.

Key Questions

  • How will overall headcount and personnel costs evolve under a hypothetical hiring freeze?
  • In which departments, critical roles, or locations are we at risk of losing essential capabilities due to turnover or retirement?
  • How much natural turnover headroom can be redirected toward growth roles instead of straight replacements?
  • What is the actual hiring volume required to hit target headcount while offsetting projected attrition?

Conceptual Approach

For most organizations it is sufficient to work with aggregated forecast numbers, but if possible and relevant, build granular, role-and-location-specific forecasts based on predictable turnover and retirement trends. Use this visibility to identify where natural departures create room to shift budgets toward new strategic skills aligned with business growth. Scenario modeling also allows you to test different conditions—such as hiring freezes or early retirement programs—and instantly see their impact on headcount costs and team composition.

The SAP Business AI Platform Solution

Using the SAP Business AI Platform, organizations can deploy predictive machine learning and AI models that analyze historical employment paths, organizational structures, tenure patterns, and retirement eligibility timelines. This generates clear, understandable turnover forecasts directly for workforce planners, with outputs that write straight back into the central planning data model.

 

Step 5: Define Target Workforce Composition and Cost

Business Context

This is the core planning stage where business strategy, workforce needs, and financial boundary conditions converge. While HR facilitates the process and provides the necessary insights, senior leadership must ultimately align business strategy with future workforce demands. One hurdle to be avoided is trying to plan to granular and on too many dimensions. The result will be hundreds if now thousands of plan values to set, validate and approve. If the overall goal for the plan to create the guardrails for developing the workforce inline with the business strategy, it is enough to have a few high level entities to plan on and not get lost in micromanaging exact headcount numbers for each team. This will greatly improve the chances of implementing a successful and sustainable process. Once established, level of granularity can be added later if needed.

Key Questions

  • Which workforce segments are we growing, stabilizing, or reducing to match our business strategy?
  • Where are we expanding our headcount by location, business area or function?
  • What is the right future structure regarding team sizes, manager ratios, and individual contributors?
  • How do different business and economic scenarios impact the plan?
  • How do we balance top-down financial limits with bottom-up operational capacity?

Conceptual Approach

  • Establish Top-Down Guardrails: Executive leadership and finance set cost ceilings and strategic priorities.
  • Reconcile Top-Down and Bottom-Up: Connect operational capacity demands with executive guidance through iterative planning.
  • Factor in AI Augmentation: Identify where AI can automate tasks and augment human capacity.
  • Keep It Pragmatic: Plan at a manageable organizational level rather than trying to model dozens or hundreds of tiny entities.
  • Use Roles as the Main Proxy: Rely on roles as a practical proxy for tracking capabilities, while keeping location and grade dimensions simple to avoid unnecessary complexity.
  • Handle Skills Separately: Treat skills as a flexible dimension rather than a rigid headcount currency, applying a separate approach if detailed skill planning is required.

The SAP Business AI Platform Solution

This step centers on SAP Analytics Cloud (SAC) Planning working directly on SAP Business Data Cloud. A seamless planning model ensures as-is and plan data live in a central repository, while the collaborative features of SAC Planning help streamline the process across the organization. Ultimately, maintaining a single data repository for both current and planned data provides the foundation for efficient planning and effective monitoring of plan execution.

 

Step 6: Set Workforce Decision Guardrails and Translate into Guidelines

Business Context

Strategic workforce plans often reside in the top management ivory tower and fail to be fully operationalized in the entire organization. When plans remain abstract documents or massive numerical tables, hiring managers default to historical habits—opening like-for-like requisitions for vacated positions. To be effective, high-level strategic numbers must be translated into clear guidance for the organization: specifying exactly what roles to hire, in which locations, and with what skills, while maintaining full transparency and governance on cost budgets. 

Key Questions

  • How do we translate numerical headcount and budget plans into clear guidance for hiring managers?
  • Which roles are allowed to be hired, in which locations and on which seniority levels ?
  • What are the explicit guardrails for opening new requisitions to stay within cost budgets?
  • Which legacy roles have structured, viable reskilling pathways into more future-oriented roles and parts of the business?

Conceptual Approach

  • Translate the workforce plan into Operational Guidance: Convert abstract numerical planning tables into clear hiring rules, defining exact role profiles, approved locations, and skill priorities.
  • Establish Governance and Budget transparency: Formulate clear operating rules tied directly to cost transparency so managers know their financial budget at every point in time.
  • Develop Reskilling Pathways: Connect legacy competencies to adjacent strategic skills, giving managers practical alternatives to external sourcing.

The SAP Business AI Platform Solution

Using the SAP Business AI Platform, data and workforce strategy from HR, Business, and Finance can be brought together into a custom app built with Joule Studio. Rather than keeping high-level strategy and hiring guidelines locked in static documents, this app translates them into a system-readable format. This structured repository can then be continuously reused by apps and strategy-aware AI agents to evaluate new position requests in real time.

 

Step 7: Embed Guidance into Hiring and Talent Management Workflows

Business Context

Strategies succeed or fail at the point of operational execution. Front-line managers will often not be aware of the strategic workforce plan or guidance every time a team member leaves. Building on the strategy-aware rules established in Step 6, the goal here is to embed those guidelines directly into the everyday tools managers already use, making the strategically aligned choice clear and accessible. It is puzzling to me that this problem has not been properly addressed yet in most HRIS systems. Bringing the necessary financial and strategy information at the point of decision making for new positions or replacements is critical to ensure a scalable strategic workforce management process.

Key Questions

  • How can we evaluate hiring requests against strategic guardrails and financial cost budgets before a job requisition is posted?
  • How can managers receive real-time alternatives (like internal mobility or upskilling paths) at the exact moment a vacancy arises, keeping total costs in mind?
  • How do we ensure strategic compliance and financial control without creating bureaucratic approval bottlenecks?

Conceptual Approach

Shift from reactive, post-hiring audits to real-time guidance right when a position is created:

  • Provide workforce guidance and financial budget visibility directly at the point of decision making
  • Provide clear, automated nudges when a requested role violates location strategies, cost budgets, or seniority structures.
  • Surface viable internal candidates or reskilling options before approving external recruitment.

The SAP Business AI Platform Solution

Using Joule Studio, organizations can operationalize strategy through a dual approach: a centralized app for central approvers that brings all necessary context and financial data into one place, combined with proactive AI agents that run constantly to assist and guide talent decisions. When a manager initiates a requisition, the agent constantly guides and controls new position requests against the strategy-aware rules from Step 6, advising hiring managers on valid alternatives (such as promoting an internal candidate or adjusting location tiers) while staying strictly within financial cost boundaries.

 

Step 8: Monitor KPIs and Adjust Actions

Business Context

Strategic Workforce management is not an annual, one-time project; it is a continuous steering discipline. Without continuous monitoring of actual execution against strategic targets, organizations risk finding out eighteen months too late that headcount grew while strategic capability goals were missed. The ultimate aim is to ensure the board never has to look back years from now wondering why the agreed-upon strategy was never actually followed. At the same time, monitoring must maintain transparency over necessary exception approvals—showing where and why they occurred—so governance protects the strategy without suffocating operational agility in micromanagement.

Key Questions

  • Are we executing in line with our strategic workforce plan, or are operational hires drifting from our target workforce composition?
  • Where and why are exception approvals being made, and do they signal shifting business needs or broken processes?
  • How do we catch budget variances and headcount drift early enough to trigger required corrective actions?

Conceptual Approach

Establish a closed-loop review cycle that links monthly operational tracking with strategic recalibration:

  • Track Plan vs. Actual: Monitor headcount, total cost of workforce, and capability density against established targets.
  • Monitor Exception Metrics: Track where and why managers require policy overrides, providing visibility without resorting to heavy-handed micromanagement.
  • Drive Adjusted Actions: Feed operational learnings and variance insights straight back into the next iteration of the planning cycle.

The SAP Business AI Platform Solution

Using the SAP Business AI Platform, SAP Analytics Cloud continuously matches live operational actuals from SAP SuccessFactors and S/4 HANA Finance against the target planning models stored in SAP Business Data Cloud. Automated drift and anomaly detection flag emerging capability gaps or cost overruns early, alerting workforce planners before minor deviations turn into major issues. This closed-loop feedback ensures real-world hiring realities automatically refine future planning cycles.

 

Closing Perspective and Outlook

Looking ahead, the degree to which autonomous AI agents will further reshape or automate workforce decisions and processes remains an open question. The goal of introducing AI into strategic workforce management is not to automate away human judgment. Decisions about headcount, organizational structure, and team development directly impact livelihoods, culture, and business velocity—humans must and will remain the ultimate decision-makers.

The real opportunity with the SAP Business AI Platform lies in closing the execution gap. By unifying HR and financial data in SAP Business Data Cloud and deploying strategy-aware AI agents via Joule Studio, we can finally eliminate the friction between boardroom strategy and operational hiring - developing a workforce continuously aligned to the business strategy.

 

In upcoming follow-up posts, I will dive into the technical details and implementation patterns for specific steps across the cycle.
Which step of the approach is the most pressing and value adding in your organization today? 
Share your thoughts in the comments below, I am looking forward to your feedback.

entry.title: Joule Work：实现对话、业务洞察与 Agent 协同的一体化工作空间
entry.content:
即将推出的 Joule Work，把对话交互、业务数据查询、任务进度追踪、异常分析以及 Agent 协同能力整合至动态工作空间内。用户只需用自然语言描述业务目标，系统就会结合业务上下文自动调度所需信息与功能，支撑后续的分析与处理。完成一项工作，无需在多个应用之间来回切换。

从 Conversations 中提出问题，到 Spaces 中集中分析，再到通过 Joule Studio 扩展 AI 能力，Joule Work 将这些体验连接起来，让业务目标与后续行动紧密衔接。

注：Joule Work 暂未正式发布（GA），最终发布范围与上线时间请以 SAP 后续官方公告为准。

图示：Joule Work 将对话、业务工作空间以及开发体验整合在统一界面当中。

产品介绍：Joule Work

 

通过自然语言开启工作：Conversations

Conversations 是和 Joule 交互对话的入口。用户可以描述想要查询的信息或是希望完成的任务，在对话过程中补充筛选条件、持续追问，从而获取对应的指引与结果。对于多步骤的复杂任务，对话也可以作为进入 Spaces 的起点。

举个例子：业务人员想要了解某项任务的进展，可以先抛出问题，再基于返回的结果做进一步分析。这种交互方式让用户直接从业务问题入手，不用事先确定需要打开哪一款应用。

图示：在 Conversations 中查询退货率异常原因、查看仓库各项指标，并将分析结果转入 Space。

 

围绕单一任务集中开展工作：Spaces

Spaces 是围绕特定业务目标搭建的动态工作空间，它会把相关的数据、工具和业务上下文汇聚在同一个环境里，并且根据当前任务动态调整展示内容。适合那些需要持续分析、多项对比或者分多步推进的工作场景，全程保留业务关注点与上下文信息。

以财务关账为例，财务负责人可以从“本月关账遇到了哪些阻碍”这个问题开始，在同一个工作空间查看相关数据、待办事项、异常信息以及 Agent 的活动记录，判断哪些事项需要优先处理，再结合已启用的能力推进后续工作。

图示：Spaces 在工作空间内汇总各个国家、仓库的退货率图表，同时你还可以在右侧继续对话、补充分析。

 

基于业务需求进行扩展开发：Develop / Joule Studio

如果企业团队需要构建专属 AI 能力，可以从 Joule Work 的左侧导航栏进入 Joule Studio。业务人员和开发人员可在 Joule Studio 中搭建适配自身业务流程的 Agents、应用以及自动化流程。

 

Joule Work、Assistant 和 Agent 的协作关系

Joule Work 是用户输入目标、查看信息、推进各项工作的交互界面；Joule Assistants 结合业务角色与流程上下文进行任务统筹；Joule Agents 负责执行专项任务，调用对应的数据、工具以及应用完成工作。

简单来说：用户在 Joule Work 中提出业务目标，由 Assistant 统筹调度所需能力，再由 Agents 执行具体任务，用户查看结果并按需做出决策。企业原有业务系统依旧承担核心业务处理工作。

企业现有的数据权限、业务授权以及审核机制保持不变。Joule Work 只是对接这些能力的交互界面，底层管控能力依托 SAP Business AI Platform；自动化程度需要结合具体业务场景进行配置。

entry.title: Building an AI-Powered SAP BASIS Operations Assistant with MCP, Python and PyRFC
entry.content:
1. Introduction

What if SAP BASIS administrators/consultants could ask an AI assistant “Are there any ST22 dumps today?”, “Which background jobs failed?”, or “Show me the busiest users in ST03N”, and receive live data from an SAP system rather than generic troubleshooting advice?

This article documents a working proof of concept that connects ChatGPT to an on-premise SAP S/4HANA 2023 system through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), Python, PyRFC and SAP NetWeaver RFC SDK. The integration currently exposes six read-oriented operational tools. It does not require SAP BTP, SAP Cloud Connector or OData for its RFC-based architecture.

The focus is reproducible architecture, actual implementation details, lessons learned and the security boundaries needed before considering production deployment.

2. Architecture

The MCP listener is bound to loopback, not the VM LAN interface. This reduces direct network exposure, but does not itself authenticate remote users. The tested plugin was configured without authentication; that setting is appropriate only for a tightly controlled PoC, not a shared or production service.

3. Tested environment

The following components were used in the working proof of concept:

SAP System: SAP S/4HANA 2023, SID S4D, ABAP 7.58, SAP HANA, client 100.

SAP Application Instance: Instance number 01, private lab network.

MCP Server: Rocky Linux 9.8 running on Microsoft Hyper-V.

Python Runtime: Python 3.11 virtual environment.

PyRFC: Version 3.4.

SAP NetWeaver RFC SDK: Version 7.50, PL20.

MCP Python SDK: Version 2.3.0.

MCP Transport: Streamable HTTP, listening on 127.0.0.1:8000/mcp.

SAP RFC User: Dedicated technical user (MCP_RFC).

Linux Service Accounts: sapmcp for the HTTP service and mcpadmin for the tunnel service.

This configuration was validated in a dedicated lab environment and should be treated as a proof of concept rather than a production-ready deployment.

4. Preparing the Linux environment

The installation uses /opt/sap-mcp. The commands below are safe verification commands for the actual environment, not a reconstructed history of every dnf or pip operation.

Project structure, omitting backup files, logs, credentials and the virtual environment:

/opt/sap-mcp/
  app/
    server.py
    server_http.py
    test_mcp.py
    test_mcp_http.py
  config/
    sap.env              # private; never publish contents
  packages/
    pyrfc-3.4-cp311-cp311-linux_x86_64.whl
  venv/
  tests/
    test_rfc.py

For a new installation, install the SAP NetWeaver RFC SDK using SAP-authorized distribution and its supported platform instructions. Install a Python version compatible with the chosen PyRFC wheel, and ensure the RFC SDK shared libraries are discoverable by the service process. The original package installation transcript and runtime library-path settings were not preserved in the reviewed documentation; therefore this article does not invent exact commands for those steps.

5. SAP RFC connection and credential handling

A dedicated technical SAP user in client 100 is used for RFC calls. Credentials are loaded from a private environment file outside the source code. Example variable names (values intentionally omitted):

SAP_ASHOST=<sap-application-host>
SAP_SYSNR=01
SAP_CLIENT=100
SAP_USER=<dedicated-rfc-user>
SAP_PASSWORD=<secret>
SAP_LANG=EN

sudo stat -c "%U %G %a %n" /opt/sap-mcp/config/sap.env

The working deployment uses restrictive permissions (mode 600). Never paste the actual environment file into a blog, issue tracker, AI prompt or screenshot. Grant only required RFC and application authorizations; RFC-enabled does not automatically mean read-only, released or safe for external use.

6. MCP server design

The application registers Python functions with an MCP server named SAP-S4D-Operations using @McP.tool(). A typical tool validates input, opens a PyRFC connection, calls an SAP function module, converts the result to JSON-compatible data and closes the connection.

In the real application, connection parameters are constructed by a load_config() helper and tools are registered using the MCP decorator. Inspect SAP function signatures in SE37 and, where useful, through PyRFC function metadata. Test function behavior in SAP before exposing it as a tool.

7. HTTP entry point — verified source

This code was copied from the running /opt/sap-mcp/app/server_http.py:

import asyncio
from server import mcp
if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(
        mcp.run_streamable_http_async(
            host="127.0.0.1",
            port=8000,
            streamable_http_path="/mcp",
        )
    )

The MCP endpoint is http://127.0.0.1:8000/mcp on the Linux VM. An outbound tunnel connects this local service to the remote client integration. The public endpoint and tunnel credentials are intentionally excluded.

8. systemd services — verified configuration

Two services were confirmed active with systemctl is-active: sap-mcp-http.service and sap-mcp-tunnel.service.

8.1 HTTP service

[Unit]
Description=SAP S4D MCP HTTP Server
After=network-online.target
Wants=network-online.target
[Service]
Type=simple
User=sapmcp
Group=sapmcp
WorkingDirectory=/opt/sap-mcp/app
ExecStart=/opt/sap-mcp/venv/bin/python /opt/sap-mcp/app/server_http.py
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=5
UMask=0077
NoNewPrivileges=true
[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

8.2 Tunnel service

The following represents the verified service with the local tunnel profile name generalized for publication. A tunnel client must be installed and provisioned separately; its configuration is provider-specific.

[Unit]
Description=Tunnel Client for SAP S4D MCP
Wants=network-online.target
After=network-online.target sap-mcp-http.service
Requires=sap-mcp-http.service
[Service]
Type=simple
User=mcpadmin
Group=mcpadmin
WorkingDirectory=/home/mcpadmin
Environment=HOME=/home/mcpadmin

The path to runtime.env is shown only as a configuration location. Do not publish its contents. The service naming and tunnel executable are specific to this PoC; adapt them to the tunnel provider used in your environment.

sudo systemctl is-active sap-mcp-http.service sap-mcp-tunnel.service
sudo systemctl status sap-mcp-http.service --no-pager
sudo systemctl status sap-mcp-tunnel.service --no-pager
sudo ss -lntp | grep :8000
sudo journalctl -u sap-mcp-http.service -n 80 --no-pager

9. The six implemented SAP operations tools

MCP toolSAP capability / implementation
sap_system_infoRFC_SYSTEM_INFO: system metadata
sap_background_jobsBAPI_XMI_LOGON + BAPI_XBP_JOB_SELECT: background jobs
sap_st22_dumpsZ_MCP_ST22_READ: ST22 dumps via internal SAP FM
sap_logged_on_usersActive SAP user sessions; exact SAP FM omitted pending source verification
sap_work_processesTH_WPINFO: work process overview (SM50)
sap_workload_statisticsSWNC_COLLECTOR_GET_AGGREGATES: ST03N daily workload

All six tools have been exercised in the PoC. This table describes operational monitoring, not a generic authorization to execute arbitrary commands or modify SAP data.

10. ST22: a custom RFC-enabled ABAP wrapper

The standard RS_ST22_GET_DUMPS function was not callable directly over RFC in this environment. A custom Remote-Enabled Function Module Z_MCP_ST22_READ was therefore created in function group ZMCP_MONITOR. The PoC used local package $TMP, which is not transportable.

The confirmed ABAP implementation is reproduced below; the FM interface includes IV_DATE, EV_COUNT and ET_DUMPS with types defined in the SAP system:

FUNCTION Z_MCP_ST22_READ.
  DATA: lv_date TYPE sy-datum,
        lt_dumps TYPE rsdumptab.
  CLEAR ev_count.
  REFRESH et_dumps.
  lv_date = iv_date.
  IF lv_date IS INITIAL.
    lv_date = sy-datum.
  ENDIF.
  CALL FUNCTION 'RS_ST22_GET_DUMPS'
    EXPORTING p_day = lv_date
    IMPORTING p_infotab = lt_dumps
    EXCEPTIONS no_authority = 1 OTHERS = 2.
  IF sy-subrc <> 0.
    RETURN.
  ENDIF.
  LOOP AT lt_dumps INTO DATA(ls_dump).
    APPEND ls_dump TO et_dumps.
  ENDLOOP.
  ev_count = lines( et_dumps ).
ENDFUNCTION.

Important limitation: this PoC code returns zero results for both an empty dump list and some failures, including authorization errors. A production wrapper must explicitly propagate errors, validate input, apply authorization checks and avoid returning sensitive dump content unnecessarily.

11. ST03N workload statistics: implementation and validation

The newest tool, sap_workload_statistics(date, top_n=10), reads daily workload aggregates through SWNC_COLLECTOR_GET_AGGREGATES. The tested parameters were COMPONENT=TOTAL, ASSIGNDSYS=S4D, PERIODTYPE=D, PERIODSTRT=<YYYYMMDD>, SUMMARY_ONLY blank, STORAGE_TYPE=A and FACTOR=1000.

The USERTCODE aggregate (DDIC structure SWNCAGGUSERTCODE) is grouped by ACCOUNT. The Python tool sums COUNT, RESPTI, CPUTI, PROCTI and QUEUETI, and converts duration units for the returned report. It validates date format and limits top_n to 1–50.

Validation: 12 October 2026Observed result
Test accountDDIC
Dialog steps8,877
Total response time2,710.256 seconds
Average response time305.31 ms
Total CPU time743.270 seconds
SAP FM records read142

The figures were cross-checked against the SAP GUI ST03N display for the same date and account. Subsequent live MCP tests returned 46,189 total steps for 12 October and 46,429 for 13 October. These are daily totals; the current tool does not establish the busiest hour.

12. Testing end to end

Validate Python syntax, restart the HTTP service after code changes, and run the MCP HTTP test script:

sudo -u sapmcp -H /opt/sap-mcp/venv/bin/python -m py_compile /opt/sap-mcp/app/server.py
sudo systemctl restart sap-mcp-http.service
sudo systemctl status sap-mcp-http.service --no-pager
sudo -u sapmcp -H /opt/sap-mcp/venv/bin/python /opt/sap-mcp/app/test_mcp_http.py

A previously confirmed HTTP test returned the MCP tool list and RFC system information (S4D, ABAP 758, HDB, client 100). After registering new tools, refresh the tool list in the ChatGPT MCP plugin configuration; otherwise the client may continue showing a cached list.

Suggested test prompts: “Show ST22 dumps for 2026-10-13”; “List background jobs for today”; “Show current work processes”; “Summarize ST03N workload for 2026-10-12, top 5 users.” Results depend on RFC authorizations and available SAP data.

13. Troubleshooting lessons

Non-RFC-enabled SAP functions: a direct remote call may produce CALL_FUNCTION_NOT_REMOTE. Verify the FM attributes in SE37; where justified, create a narrow, audited RFC wrapper rather than assuming an internal FM is remotely callable.

Tool visibility: a successful server restart does not necessarily update the ChatGPT plugin tool catalog. Refresh tools and rerun the listing test.

Python decorator behavior: in this implementation, a registered tool function can be called directly for a local test; do not assume it has an .fn property.

ST03N aggregation: match the aggregation period, component and SAP GUI filters before comparing results. A daily aggregate cannot answer a peak-hour question.

14. Security and production readiness

This is a functional PoC, not a production-certified integration. Before deployment to clients, implement authenticated access to the MCP endpoint (for example OAuth/OIDC where supported), per-user and per-system authorization, least-privilege SAP technical users, controlled tool allowlists, auditing, rate limits, secret rotation, network segmentation and response redaction.

For potentially destructive operations such as restart, backup, user administration or job cancellation, introduce explicit approval gates, scoped permissions, precondition checks and change logs. Never expose arbitrary RFC or operating-system command execution merely because an AI client can call tools.

Review SAP support and release status for each function module. Internal SAP FMs may change across releases and are not equivalent to stable public APIs.

15. Next steps

Planned extensions include RFC metadata discovery, SM12 locks, SM21 system logs, ST02/ST06 performance monitoring, hourly ST03N time profiles, and a multi-system gateway with strict system-level isolation. A separate SAP BTP/OData-based MCP integration is also being considered; it has not been implemented as part of this RFC PoC.

16. Conclusion

MCP provides a practical interface between conversational AI and SAP BASIS operations. In this PoC, Python and PyRFC translate six well-defined monitoring tasks into SAP RFC calls, while Streamable HTTP and an outbound tunnel connect the Linux gateway to ChatGPT. The key engineering lesson is to validate SAP APIs, restrict privileges and verify results against SAP GUI before trusting AI-generated operational summaries.

entry.title: Provisioning an SAP Cloud Identity Services Tenant via Self-Service Request in SAP for Me
entry.content:
SAP Cloud Identity Services · How-To

Provisioning an SAP Cloud Identity Services Tenant via Self-Service Request in SAP for Me

A practical, step-by-step walkthrough of requesting your test or production tenant directly from SAP's central customer portal — no support ticket required.

🗓️ Updated October 2026 ⏱️ ~8 min read 👤For SAP administrators & S-user holders

SAP Cloud Identity Services is the backbone for authentication, single sign-on, and identity provisioning across your SAP landscape. Before you can configure any of that, you need a tenant. This guide shows you how to request one yourself through SAP for Me — SAP's central customer portal for managing products, systems, and entitlements.

Before you start: do you already have a tenant? A tenant may already have been created for you automatically as part of a bundle with an SAP cloud solution. Always check first — if a tenant exists and you are one of its administrators, go straight to the Administration Console instead of requesting a new one. New tenants are created only if there are no existing tenants bound to your Customer ID.

What's in this guide

  1. Prerequisites
  2. Two starting points in SAP for Me
  3. Flow A — Get a tenant from Portfolio & Products (step-by-step)
  4. Flow B — Get a tenant from Systems & Provisioning (bundled)
  5. After provisioning & next steps

00. Prerequisites

What you need Details
An S-user IDWith your SAP for Me credentials and the appropriate authorizations to request/provision systems for your Customer ID.
Confirmed there's no existing tenantCheck View Assigned Tenants and Administrators. A tenant is reused across SAP cloud solutions — you usually want one productive tenant for out-of-the-box SSO.
Know your regionFor EU Access contracts, pick a tenant located in Europe. Region choice affects performance and compliance.
A target resource group (Flow A)You'll select a Path to a resource group during the wizard.

01. Two starting points in SAP for Me

SAP for Me offers two different dashboards from which you can obtain a tenant. Pick the one that matches your scenario:

Dashboard Use it when…
Portfolio & Products
The commercial catalog of what you purchased		You want to explicitly request a test or production tenant for integration with SAP-managed cloud ERP applications, Joule, and other supported solutions. The tenant comes with SAP-managed integration configurations. → Flow A
Systems & Provisioning
Where you view, request, activate & manage cloud tenants		You're provisioning an SAP cloud solution and want a tenant bundled with it, preconfigured and in the same region. The tenant is created automatically as part of that request. → Flow B

02. Flow A — Request a tenant from Portfolio & Products

This is the classic self-service "Get Tenant" path. Follow the steps below.

1. Log on to SAP for Me and open the Portfolio & Products dashboard

Sign in at me.sap.com with your S-user ID and password, then open the Portfolio & Products dashboard.

SAP for Me landing page — the Portfolio & Products dashboard.
2. Go to the My Product Packages tab and select the SAP Cloud Identity Services tile

Open the My Product Packages tab, then click the SAP Cloud Identity Services tile to open its details.

Selecting the SAP Cloud Identity Services tile under My Product Packages.
3. Open the Applications tab and choose Start Provisioning

Inside the product, switch to the Applications tab. On the SAP Cloud Identity Services tile, choose Start Provisioning. The Create Solution wizard launches.

The Applications tab — choose "Start Provisioning" to launch the Create Solution wizard.
4. Fill in General Information

In the first step of the wizard, provide the following and then choose Next Step:

  • Entitlement System — read-only; displays the system ID of SAP Cloud Identity.
  • Name — a unique name for the solution. Max 63 characters, lowercase letters, numbers, hyphens and periods only; must start and end with a letter or number.
  • Path — use the Value Help to select a path to a resource group.
  • Business Type — choose Test or Production.
You can't rename a solution after you create it. Decide on the name carefully before moving on.
Step 1 — General Information. Entitlement System is pre-filled; you set Name, Path and Business Type.
5. Configure parameters — select a region

In the Configure Parameters step, select the region where the tenant will be hosted, then choose Review.

Step 2 — Configure Parameters. Pick the hosting region for the tenant.
6. Review your entries and choose Finish

On the Review step, double-check everything — especially the Name and Business Type, which can't be changed later — then choose Finish. Your provisioning request starts immediately.

Step 3 — Review and Finish. The request is submitted the moment you confirm.
7. Track status on the Resources tab until it's Ready

Provisioning takes a few moments. The solution resource reaches Ready status only when all tenants are successfully provisioned and the integrations are fully established. Monitor progress on the Resources tab. You can find out the tenant address within the detail page.

The Resources tab — watch each resource move from In Progress to Ready.
 
Done! Once the tenant is provisioned, you can proceed to provision your SAP cloud applications — the new SAP Cloud Identity tenant will be available for selection during that process.
 

03. Flow B — Get a tenant from Systems & Provisioning (bundled)

Use this flow when you want a tenant bundled with an SAP cloud solution e.g. SAP Cloud ALM. There's no separate "request tenant" button here — when you provision your application and no SAP Cloud Identity Services tenant is available, one is created automatically when you submit the request.

Step 1 — Open Systems & Provisioning → Provisioning tab

Log on to SAP for Me, open the Systems & Provisioning dashboard, and go to the Provisioning tab.

Step 2 — Choose Start Provisioning for your solution

Under Systems to be Provisioned, choose Start Provisioning for the SAP cloud solution you want to bundle with SAP Cloud Identity Services.

If the button is disabled… automatic tenant creation isn't available for this case. You must first request a tenant manually in the SAP BTP cockpit, then return to SAP for Me and restart provisioning so the new tenant appears for selection.

Step 3 — Complete the Start New Provisioning Request dialog

Provide the following, then choose Submit:

Field What to enter
RegionThe data-center location for the solution tenant. Not available for all applications; may be system-determined by your contract.
Integration with SAP Cloud Identity ServicesSelect a test or production SAP Cloud Identity tenant. For some apps you can integrate a test application tenant with a productive identity tenant.
Owner of SAP Cloud Identity ServicesOwn systems (same Customer ID) or Shared systems (a tenant from a different Customer ID shared with your company).
Start New Provisioning Request
Start New Provisioning Request
Region
Europe (Frankfurt)▼
Integration with SAP Cloud Identity Services
ProductionTest▼
Owner of SAP Cloud Identity Services
Own systemsShared systems▼
CancelSubmit
The Start New Provisioning Request dialog — a tenant is auto-created on Submit if none exists.

04. After provisioning & next steps

  • Activate your tenant. Depending on the path, you may receive an account activation email. Open it, follow the link, set your administrator password, and continue into the Administration Console.
  • A self-service tenant is not preconfigured. You must configure it for your specific authentication and provisioning scenario (identity sources, SSO, provisioning targets, etc.).
  • Reuse before you request. For out-of-the-box SSO between SAP cloud solutions, use a single productive tenant wherever possible.
  • Special cases: multi-region businesses can request additional per-region tenants; each SAP SuccessFactors instance should get its own tenant via the SuccessFactors Upgrade Center.
Products delivered on SAP BTP? Products running on a customer-managed SAP BTP subaccount usually don't trigger automatic tenant creation — you request the tenant in the SAP BTP cockpit instead. On an SAP-managed subaccount, the tenant is provisioned automatically with the application.
Written as a how-to guide for SAP administrators. UI mockups are illustrative — replace the dashed slots with real screenshots from your environment before publishing.
Source: SAP Help Portal — Get Your Tenant (SAP Cloud Identity Services). Always confirm against the latest official documentation.

entry.title: Re: ABAP syntax advice
entry.content:
@jeff_broodwar for sample 2, if <fs_bukrs> and r_bukrs are both ranges of BUKRS, as the loop suggests, yes, row 11 is the one I would use. "Always" needs two conditions, though.

First, row 11 replaces and the loop adds. APPEND keeps what was already in r_bukrs, and the assignment deletes it first. The ABAP documentation of the conversion rules for internal tables says it directly: "When assigning an internal table to another, the lines of the target table are deleted." If r_bukrs is empty at that point, there is no difference. If you collect values from more than one place, you need to add, and then APPEND LINES OF <fs_bukrs> TO r_bukrs does in one line what rows 1 to 9 do.

Second, the line types must be the same. Row 11 doesn't look at the component names. I tried a range of BUKRS into a range of KUNNR in my S/4HANA 2023 lab, and the syntax check gives 0 errors and 0 warnings. But the row is moved as one block of characters, by position. Reading the conversion rule for flat structures, an interval 1000 to 1999 would arrive with LOW = 10001999 and an empty HIGH. The loop with VALUE #, or CORRESPONDING #( ) as ERPClimb showed, go by name and don't have this problem. For this part I only did the syntax check, I didn't run it.

So my rule of thumb: same type and you want to replace, row 11. Same type and you want to add, APPEND LINES OF. Different types, CORRESPONDING.

entry.title: Re: Advanced Intercompany Stock Transfer (5HP) in SAP S4HANA Cloud Public Edition
entry.content:
@Rajubothra 

Unfortunately, SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition does not provide a standard configuration to automatically park invoices before posting — auto-generated invoices (via ERS, EDI, or API) are posted directly to FI with no out-of-the-box "park-first" intercept.

However, the Stochastic Block mechanism can be leveraged as a compensating control:

  • By setting the blocking probability to 100% with a threshold of zero, every posted supplier invoice is automatically assigned a payment block (reason code R).
  • The invoice is posted to accounting, but payment is fully prevented until a finance team member explicitly releases it via the Release Blocked Invoices Fiori app.
  • This configuration is available as a standard Self-Service Configuration UI (SSCUI) in Public Cloud under: Manage Your Solution → Procurement → Logistics Invoice Verification → Set Stochastic Block.

The practical outcome is equivalent in terms of payment control: no invoice can be paid without a deliberate human review and release step, which satisfies the core intent of the requirement — even though the interception point is at payment rather than at posting.

Trade-off to be aware of: since the invoice is already posted, the FI document and GR/IR clearing entry exist before the review. If the invoice needs to be rejected after review, it must be reversed rather than simply discarded — a slightly heavier process compared to rejecting a parked document.

entry.title: Re: Update Tax Liable for Consolidated BP's
entry.content:
Hi Brian,

That message (Tax status of summary BP not permitted [OCRD.FatherCard]) is SAP Business One checking that a business partner and its consolidating BP have the same tax status. KBA 3468667 covers it. Because the check runs on every single update, you hit it in both directions: change the consolidating BP first and it no longer matches its children; change a child first and it no longer matches the parent. That's why DTW and the UI both refuse.

The way around it is to break the link temporarily, change the tax status, then put the link back:

1. Take a snapshot of the families before touching anything, so you can restore the links exactly:

SELECT T0."CardCode", T0."CardName", T0."FatherCard", T0."FatherType", T0."VatStatus"

FROM OCRD T0

WHERE T0."FatherCard" IS NOT NULL

   OR T0."CardCode" IN (SELECT "FatherCard" FROM OCRD WHERE "FatherCard" IS NOT NULL)

ORDER BY COALESCE(T0."FatherCard", T0."CardCode"), T0."CardCode"

FatherType tells you whether each link is payment consolidation or delivery consolidation, so keep it.

2. On each child BP, remove the consolidating BP (Accounting tab > General, Consolidating BP). If there are many, do one record first through DTW to confirm your DTW version actually clears the field from your template. If it doesn't, do the unlinking in the UI or with a small DI API / Service Layer update.

3. Update the tax status (Accounting tab > Tax) on all of them, parents and children, to Exempt. Now there's no parent/child pair to compare, so this works through DTW as normal (BusinessPartners object, VatLiable field).

4. Re-link each child to its consolidating BP with the original FatherType from your snapshot.

5. Run the query from step 1 again and compare it with the snapshot.

Two things to check before you do it in production:

- If any of these links are payment consolidation, check the open A/R items for those customers first and avoid doing this while incoming payments are being entered for them. Test how open items look on the copy database after unlinking and re-linking.

- Changing the BP to Exempt only changes defaults for new documents. Existing open orders and deliveries keep the tax codes they already have, so review those separately.

Try the whole sequence on a copy of the company database first.

Hello Experts,

We are facing an issue in SAP PPM/PS integration and would like to understand whether anyone has encountered similar behavior.

Scenario

When an initiative is assigned to or removed from an item through the Related Items page:

  • The initiative assignment/removal is performed successfully.
  • The initiative description is correctly displayed in the Item Overview tab.
  • However, the corresponding Initiative ID and Initiative Description in Project Builder are not refreshed automatically.

Observed Behavior

The values in Project Builder are updated only after making an additional manual change to the item (for example, modifying the item description, adding a character, and saving again).

Expected Behavior

Project Builder should reflect the latest Initiative ID and Description immediately after the initiative is assigned or removed from the Related Items page, without requiring any additional save action.

SAP Response

We raised an OSS Incident and received the following clarification from SAP:

  • SAP confirmed that DFM synchronization supports either:
    • Initiative ↔ Item synchronization, or
    • Item ↔ PS Project synchronization.
  • The combined synchronization path Initiative ↔ Item ↔ PS Project is not supported in SAP standard.
  • SAP referred to KBA 3515319 – "Synchronization isn't working between Item/PPM-Project/PS-Project".
  • SAP stated that synchronization from Initiative directly through Item to PS Project and vice versa is not delivered in standard SAP code.
  • According to SAP, the observed behavior is working as designed and is therefore not considered a bug.
  • SAP suggested submitting an enhancement request through the Customer Influence / Customer Connection process if this functionality is required in standard product behavior.

Questions

  1. Has anyone implemented a custom solution to automatically synchronize Initiative data from Item to Project Builder?
  2. Is there any BAdI, enhancement spot, event, or workflow exit that can be leveraged to trigger the synchronization?
  3. Is there any standard report, synchronization program, buffer refresh mechanism, or background job that can update Project Builder immediately after Related Item changes?
  4. Has anyone found an SAP Note or recommended workaround other than manually re-saving the item?

Any guidance, implementation experience, or best practices would be greatly appreciated.

Thank you

entry.title: The brain behind the recommendation — a guarded LLM on SAP BTP + SAP AI Core
entry.content:
A custom SAP S/4HANA AI use case, built responsibly on SAP BTP + SAP AI Core.

Part 2 of 3 — "AI‑Guided Supplier Selection in SAP S/4HANA". Part 1: the in‑transaction assistant (ME51N). This part: the SAP BTP + AI Core service that decides. Part 3: the standalone RAP + Fiori app. (Prototype / proof‑of‑concept — a custom extension, not standard/embedded functionality. System IDs, hostnames and deployment IDs are masked.)

TL;DR

In Part 1 we dropped an explainable supplier recommendation straight into ME51N's Desired Vendor field. This part answers the obvious question: how does it decide — and how do we stop an LLM from inventing a supplier or leaking data? The short answer: keep the facts in ABAP, keep the AI on a short leash. S/4 computes the KPIs and sends only a shortlist of eligible candidates; a small FastAPI service on SAP BTP builds the prompt, calls SAP AI Core, and — crucially — validates every answer server‑side so a recommended supplier that isn't one of our candidates is rejected outright. No fabricated vendors, no raw history leaving S/4.

Landscape diagram of S4, BTP and AI Core

Why not just call an LLM from ABAP?

You could POST a prompt to a model and parse whatever comes back. In procurement, that's a bad idea for three reasons:

  • Hallucination — a model might confidently name a supplier you never sourced from, or make up a KPI. In a purchase requisition, that's not a quirky demo — it's a wrong PO.
  • Data residency & trust — you don't want raw purchase‑order and goods‑receipt history flowing to an external endpoint.
  • Explainability — a bare "use vendor X" with no reason is one a buyer will (rightly) ignore.

So the design draws a hard line between what must be deterministic (the numbers) and what the AI is actually good at (ranking and explaining in natural language) — and it puts a validation gate between the model and the business.

The split: ABAP computes, the service reasons

On the S/4 side, ZCL_VENDORREC_SERVICE reads the procurement facts for a material and computes, per supplier, the KPIs that matter — on‑time rate, fill rate, average delay — plus a weighted baseline score and rank. Only that shortlist of eligible candidates (a supplier is eligible if it has real history for the material) is sent onward. The raw history never leaves the system.

The BTP service receives those candidates and does the AI‑specific work: prompt → call → validate → derive sourcing. If anything goes wrong, it returns a status, never a guess.

Responsible AI in one line: the model may only rank and explain the candidates we send it — it cannot add, invent, or alter a supplier. Everything else is deterministic ABAP or server‑side checks.

How it works (technical deep‑dive)

From here on it's for the developers. If you're here for the concept, skip to “What's next”.

The contract

S/4 calls one endpoint — POST /recommend — with the candidates; the service returns per‑material recommendations plus a sourcing scenario:

Request : { consolidation_preference, price_intelligence_available, materials:[ { material,
             suppliers:[ { supplier, is_eligible, baseline_score,
                           on_time_rate, fill_rate, avg_delay_days, …, data_warning } ] } ] }
Response: { ai_status, materials:[ { recommended_supplier, recommendation_reason,
             alternative_suppliers[], recommendation_confidence, … } ],
             sourcing_scenario: { type: COMMON|SPLIT, supplier_count, coverage_pct, assignments[] } }

Note what the request is not: no PO numbers, no receipts, no prices — just aggregated metrics per supplier. (price_intelligence_available is false in V1 — price KPIs are deliberately out of scope, so the model reasons on delivery performance only.)

The prompt keeps the model on a leash

The system prompt is explicit about the rules: recommend only from the supplied eligible candidates for each material, don't invent suppliers or KPIs, justify every pick, and respect the buyer's consolidation preference. It asks for strict JSON only:

You are a procurement sourcing advisor. For EACH material recommend the best supplier ONLY from
that material's supplied eligible candidates. Do not invent suppliers, KPI values, or facts…
Return the top alternative suppliers (up to 4), each with a specific 1–2 sentence reason…
Respond with VALID JSON ONLY: { "materials":[ { "recommended_supplier":"", "recommendation_reason":"",
"alternative_suppliers":[…], "recommendation_confidence":"HIGH|MEDIUM|LOW" } ] }

But a prompt is a request, not a guarantee. The guarantee comes next.

The guarantee: server‑side validation

Every response is validated before it's trusted. If the model names a supplier that isn't in the candidate set for that material — or repeats one, or returns an unknown confidence value — the entire response is rejected and the service returns AI_RESPONSE_INVALID. This is the single most important piece of the whole design:

def _validate(parsed: dict, req: RecommendRequest) -> bool:
    # supplier ids we actually sent, per material
    elig = {m.material: {s.supplier for s in m.suppliers if s.is_eligible} for m in req.materials}
    for r in parsed.get("materials", []):
        mat = r.get("material")
        if mat not in elig:
            return False
        rec = r.get("recommended_supplier")
        if not rec or rec not in elig[mat]:          # <- the anti-hallucination gate
            return False
        if r.get("recommendation_confidence") not in ("HIGH", "MEDIUM", "LOW"):
            return False
        seen = {rec}
        for a in r.get("alternative_suppliers", []) or []:
            sid = a.get("supplier")
            if not sid or sid not in elig[mat] or sid in seen:
                return False
            seen.add(sid)
    return True

Because of this gate, the ABAP side can trust that whatever it defaults into the Desired Vendor is a real, eligible supplier — the model gets to be persuasive, never creative with facts.

Single vs. multi‑material: COMMON or SPLIT

For a single PR line the service just returns the per‑material pick (this is the path Part 1 uses). When several materials are requested together, it derives a sourcing scenario deterministically from the validated picks — never left to the LLM:

  • COMMON — one supplier can cover all materials → a single purchase order.
  • SPLIT — no common supplier (or the preference favors best‑fit) → one PO per supplier group.

The consolidation preference is the buyer's lever: CONSOLIDATE (favor one supplier), BEST_FIT (best per material), or BALANCED (consolidate only when the shared supplier stays within ~80% of the best‑per‑material score). supplier_count in the result is literally the number of POs.

Flowchart of the recommend service decision path

When the AI is unavailable or wrong

There is no silent fabrication. Transport/timeout errors → AI_UNAVAILABLE; malformed or invalid JSON → AI_RESPONSE_INVALID. ABAP treats both as "no AI answer" and falls back to the best supplier by history (flagged BASELINE in Part 1). A truncated model response (hit the token limit) is also treated as invalid rather than half‑trusted.

Secure by construction: S/4 → BTP → AI Core

The call chain is authenticated end‑to‑end:

  1. S/4 gets an OAuth2 token from XSUAA (via the SM59 destination — client credentials).
  2. It calls the service over HTTPS with the Bearer token (TLS trust via STRUST).
  3. The BTP app validates the JWT against XSUAA before doing any work.
  4. The app reads its AI Core credentials from a bound service (never in code) and calls the model.

Sequence diagram of the secured call chain

Secrets live only where they belong — the AI Core key in the BTP service binding, the OAuth client secret in the SM59 destination — and only aggregated KPIs ever cross the boundary.

Setting this up yourself? The click‑by‑click for the OAuth 2.0 client‑credentials profile, the STRUST certificate import, and the SM59 destination is standard connectivity, not specific to this use case — so I won't repeat it here. On help.sap.com search "Maintaining OAuth 2.0 Client Profiles" and "Trust Manager (STRUST)"; on SAP Community search "consume BTP API from ABAP OAuth 2.0 client credentials SM59" for step‑by‑step walkthroughs.

A deployment note

This prototype runs gpt‑4o‑mini via SAP AI Core orchestration — swap in whatever model your AI Core hub serves. Richer per‑supplier reasons mean more output tokens, so watch the model's max‑tokens setting: too low and long multi‑material responses get truncated (→ AI_RESPONSE_INVALID). It's an env‑var, not a code change. A mock mode (deterministic top‑baseline, no model call) is handy for local dev and demos without credentials.

What's next

We've now covered the buyer's experience (Part 1) and the brain that powers it (this part). In Part 3 we look at the standalone RAP + Fiori Elements app — the "explore" surface where a buyer can run recommendations across a whole basket of materials, see the COMMON/SPLIT sourcing, and tune the consolidation preference — all on the same engine.

How are you keeping LLMs honest in your SAP scenarios — prompt discipline, server‑side validation, something else? We'd love to compare notes in the comments.
