entry.title: Comprehensive guide for configuring and testing 2-step Intercompany STO process with Dlv Ty NCC3
entry.content:
This blog is intended to enable FICO/MM consultants to successfully configure intercompany STO process with delivery type NCC3(stock transfer from the valuated stock in transit of the issuing plant via the valuated stock in transit of the receiving plant to the unrestricted-use stock of the receiving plant) and run an end to end test based on the setup.

Content:

Part A. Configuration Overview:

Part B. Configuration Detail:

Part C. Data Preparation:

Part D. Defects and Solutions

We developed the configurations, master data, and transactional documents in this guide within an SAP S/4HANA 2020 On-Premise (FPS0) environment.

 

Part A. Configuration Overview:

  1. Define (Purchasing) Document Types(ZNB2)
  2. Define Shipping Data for Plants(Receiving Plant 1310 -> Customer No. IC1310, Supplying Plant 1710 -> Sales Organization 1710 + Distribution Channel 10 + Division 00)
  3. Assign Document Type, One-Step Procedure, Underdelivery Tolerance (Supplying Plant 1710 +Receiving Plant 1310 -> STO Document Type ZNB2)
  4. Configure Delivery Type & Availability Check Procedure by Plant(Purchasing Document Type ZNB2 + Supplying Plant 1710 -> Delivery Type NCC3 + Checking Rule B)
  5. Define Item Category Determination in Deliveries( Delivery Type NCC3 + Item Category Group NORM from Material Master Data + Usage V is constant for STO -> Item Category NCC3)
  6. Define Schedule Line Categories( Schedule Line Category N3 -> Movement type 681 & 685)
  7. Assign Schedule Line Categories( Item Category NCC3 + MRP Type Blank -> Schedule Line Category N3 )
  8. Maintain Copying Control for Billing Documents （Tgt IV <- Source NCC3 ）
  9. Define MM Condition Type(PI01) and SD Condition Type (PI01, Refer to MM Condition Type PI01)
  10. Partner Determination Procedure(For Customer/Delivery/Billing)
  11. Define and Assign (SD) Pricing Procedure(To Billing Type IV) （Sales Organization 1310 +Distribution Channel 10+Division 00+ Doc.Pricing Proc. 01+ Cust.Pricing Proc. 02 = Pricing Procedure Y17J01 ）
  12. Set Calculation Schema-Purchasing(A13001)
  13. Define Schema Determination (Schema GrpPOrg 1310 + Sch.Grp Supp -> Calculation Schema A13001)
  14. Maintain Output Types(SPED)
  15. Maintain Output Determination Procedure (Output Determination Procedure V10000 -> Output Type SPED)
  16. Assign Output Determination Procedure(Delivery Type NCC3 -> Output Determination Procedure V10000 )
  17. Define Order Confirmations for Inbound Deliveries(Purchasing Document Category F + Order Type (Purchasing) ZNB2 + Plant 1310 + Storage Location 131C -> Confirmation Control Key 0004)
  18. Set Up Confirmation Control (Key 0004 -> Category LA )
  19. Define Internal Confirmation Categories (Confirmation Category LA -> Delivery Type EL + ELST)
  20. Define Item Category Determination in Deliveries(Delivery Type ELST + Item Category NORM + Usage V -> Item Category ELST)
  21. Define (Inbound) Delivery Item Categories(Item Category ELST -> Movement Type 109)
  22. Change Movement Type(Movement Type 685 -> GBB-VAY)
  23. Define Default Account Assignment(Activate PrfSeg for G/L Account corresponding to GBB-VAY)

 

Part B. Configuration Detail:

 

1 Define (Purchasing) Document Types

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Materials Management -> Purchasing -> Purchase Order -> Define Document Types for Purchase Orders

 

2 Define Shipping Data for Plants

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Materials Management -> Purchasing -> Purchase Order -> Set up Stock Transport Order -> Define Shipping Data for Plants

Parameters for Receiving Plant

Plant: Enter the receiving plant, in our case 1310.

Customer No Plant: Enter the customer code IC1310, which was previously created to represent the plant of company 1310.
*Note: Since company 1310 acts as the receiving/purchasing party (i.e., the customer of company 1710's plant) in this demo scenario, this field must not be left blank.

SlsOrg.Int.B (Sales Organization for Intercompany Billing): Leave blank or enter the sales organization of 1310.
*Note: Since company 1310 acts as the receiving/purchasing party instead of the supplying/selling party in this demo scenario, this field can be left blank in this context.

DistChannelIB (Distribution Channel for Intercompany Billing): Leave blank or enter the distribution channel of 1310.
*Note: Since company 1310 acts as the receiving/purchasing party instead of the supplying/selling party in this demo scenario, this field can be left blank in this context.

Div.Int.Billing (Division for Intercompany Billing): Leave blank or enter the division of 1310.
*Note: Since company 1310 acts as the receiving/purchasing party instead of the supplying/selling party in this demo scenario, this field can be left blank in this context.

Parameters for Supplying Plant

 Plant: Enter the supplying plant, in our case 1710.

Customer No Plant: Leave this blank or enter IC1710 (provided that the customer master record IC1710 has already been created).
*Note: Entering IC1710 here means that when plant 1710 procures goods from other affiliated plants within the group, IC1710 will serve as the Customer on the STO (specifically in the Customer field under the Shipping tab in the Item Details section). Since company 1710 acts as the supplying/selling plant (not the receiving/purchasing plant) in this demo scenario, leaving this field blank will not affect the process. However, if plant 1710 needs to function as a receiving party in an STO, you must enter the customer code representing plant 1710 (e.g., IC1710) here.

SlsOrg.Int.B (Sales Organization for Intercompany Billing): Enter the sales organization of 1710.
*Note: Because company 1710 acts as the supplying/selling party in this demo scenario, entering the sales organization of 1710 is mandatory in this context.

DistChannelIB (Distribution Channel for Intercompany Billing): Enter the distribution channel of 1710.
*Note: Because company 1710 acts as the supplying/selling party in this demo scenario, entering the distribution channel of 1710 is mandatory in this context.

Div.Int.Billing (Division for Intercompany Billing): Enter the division of 1710.
*Note: Because company 1710 acts as the supplying/selling party in this demo scenario, entering the division of 1710 is mandatory in this context.                 

 

3 Assign Document Type, One-Step Procedure, Underdelivery Tolerance

Supplying Plant 1710 +Receiving Plant 1310 -> STO Document Type ZNB2.

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Materials Management -> Purchasing -> Purchase Order -> Set up Stock Transport Order -> Assign Document Type, One-Step Procedure, Underdelivery Tolerance

Maintain a rule that links the supplying plant to the receiving plant and STO document Type.

SPlt: Enter the supplying plant, in our case 1710.

Plnt: Enter the receiving plant, in our case 1310.

Type: Select the purchasing document type. In our case, a custom document type ZNB1 is used.

One Step: This indicator determines whether the STO process uses a one-step or two-step procedure.

A: Checking this indicator means that goods issue and goods receipt are completed in a single action. When the supplying company 1710 posts goods issue (Tcode VL02N, Movement type 645) against the Outbound Delivery (created via tcode VL10B/VL10D), the system automatically and simultaneously posts the goods receipt (Movement type 101) for the receiving company 1310. Title of goods is transferred directly from the supplying plant (1710) to the receiving plant (1310) in one single step.

B: Deselect this indicator means a Two-step procedure): This is generally the more controlled approach. When the supplying company (1710) posts goods issue using movement type 681, unrestricted-use stock is transferred to special stock in transit (Special stock indicator T) rather than being immediately deducted from the supplying plant's stock. When ownership transfers to the purchasing company (1310) according to the agreed terms of contract between 2 parties, the supplying company executes VLPOD to reduce it's stock in transit and recognize COGS(movement type 685), both material document and accounting document would be generated. And simultaneously a goods receipt into valuated blocked stock(movement type 107) would be posted in the receiving company, both material document and accounting document would be created. Once the goods physically arrive, the receiving company posts goods receipt against the inbound delivery(movement type 109 ) to transfer valuated blocked stock to unrestricted stock, a material document would be generated but not accounting document. The two-step approach provides clearer accountability and better traceability, although it requires an additional step.

Underdeliv.tol.: Defines the permitted tolerance for partial delivery.

Based on my project experience, the "Two-Step Procedure" is recommended for cross-company code (intercompany) transactions to ensure clear financial accounting and rigorous inventory management. Although it requires an extra step in operations, it prevents a lot of future disputes and alignment issues.

 

4 Configure Delivery Type & Availability Check Procedure by Plant

STO Document Type(ZNB2) + Supplying Plant(1710) -> Delivery Type(NCC3) + Checking Rule(B).

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Materials Management -> Purchasing -> Purchase Order -> Set up Stock Transport Order -> Configure Delivery Type & Availability Check Procedure by Plant

Ty.：Enter the purchase document type defined for intercompany STO, such as ZNB2.

SPl: Enter the supplying plant,  in our example 1710

DlTy.：Select NCC3

CRl：Enter B

*This setting tells SAP to use the delivery process associated with delivery type NCC3 when an STO of type ZNB2 is created.

 

5 Define Item Category Determination in Deliveries

Delivery Type(NCC3) + Item Category Group(NORM from Material Master Data) + Usage(V is for STO) -> Item Category (NCC3)

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Logistics Execution -> Shipping -> Deliveries -> Define Item Category Determination in Deliveries

This Logistics Execution (LE) configuration determines the delivery item category automatically from delivery type NCC3, item category group NORM, and usage V.

 

6 Define Schedule Line Categories

Schedule Line Category(N3) -> Movement Type 681 & 685

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Sales and Distribution -> Sales -> Sales Documents -> Schedule Lines -> Define Schedule Line Categories.

When the supplying company (1710) posts goods issue in VL02N, movement type 681 transfers unrestricted-use stock to stock in transit (T stock). When the supplying company executes VLPOD, movement type 685 reduces stock in transit and recognizes the cost of goods sold (COGS).

 

7 Assign Schedule Line Categories

Item Category(NCC3) + MRP Type(Blank) -> Schedule Line Category(N3)

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Sales and Distribution -> Sales -> Sales Documents -> Schedule Lines -> Assign Schedule Line Categories

This setting make sure that Schedule Line Category N3 would be used when Item Category is NCC2(Which links to delivery type NCC3)

 

8 Maintain Copying Control for Billing Documents (Tgt IV, Source NCC3)

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Sales and Distribution -> Billing -> Billing Documents -> Maintain Copying Control for Billing Documents

If Price Source A is selected, the receiving/purchasing company’s STO condition value would be copied into the supplying company’s billing document as its billing condition. For example, the receiving/purchasing company's purchase price can be copied as the supplying company's intercompany sales price.

 

9 Define Condition Types PI01

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Materials Management -> Purchasing -> Conditions -> Define Price Determination Process -> Define Condition Types

Create 2 separate condition types to represent the sales price for the supplying company and the purchase price for the receiving company.

MM Condition type PI01（purchase price for the receiving company）

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Sales and Distribution -> Basic Functions -> Pricing -> Pricing Control -> Define Condition Types

SD Condition Type（sales price for the supplying company）

For the SD condition type, set Ref. Condition Type to the MM condition type with the same code, which is PI01, and set Ref. Application to M. Together with Price Source A in copying control, this allows the condition from the purchasing company's STO to be copied to the supplying company's billing document.

 

10 Setup Partner Determination for Deliveries

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Sales and Distribution -> Basic Functions -> Partner Determination -> Set Up Partner Determination Delivery Type -> Partner Determination Procedure

ZNIC is the account group used for customer IC1310. Assign partner determination procedure CUST to account group ZNIC.

 

11 Define and Assign (SD) Pricing Procedure Y17J01

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Sales and Distribution -> Basic Functions -> Pricing -> Pricing Control -> Define And Assign Pricing Procedures

The screenshot below shows only two of the condition types required for this procedure as an example.

 

12 Set Calculation Schema(MM Pricing Procedure)-Purchasing A13001

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Materials Management -> Purchasing -> Conditions -> Define Price Determination Process -> Set Calculation Schema - Purchasing

 

13 Define Schema（MM Pricing Procedure）Determination

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Materials Management -> Purchasing -> Conditions -> Define Price Determination Process -> Define Schema Group

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Materials Management -> Purchasing -> Conditions -> Define Price Determination Process -> Define Schema Determination

 

14 Maintain Output Types SPED

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Logistics Execution -> Shipping -> Basic Shipping Functions -> Output Control -> Output Determination -> Maintain Output Determination for Outbound Deliveries -> Maintain Output Types

Output type SPED enables SAP to create an inbound delivery automatically for the purchasing company (1310) when goods issue is posted with reference to outbound delivery for the supplying company's (1710).

 

15 Maintain Output Determination Procedure

Output Determination Procedure V10000 -> Output Type SPED

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Logistics Execution -> Shipping -> Basic Shipping Functions -> Output Control -> Output Determination -> Maintain Output Determination for Outbound Deliveries -> Maintain Output Determination Procedure

 

16 Assign Output Determination Procedure V10000

Delivery Type NCC3 -> Output Determination Procedure V10000

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Logistics Execution -> Shipping -> Basic Shipping Functions -> Output Control -> Output Determination -> Maintain Output Determination for Outbound Deliveries -> Assign Output Determination Procedures

 

17 Define Order Confirmations for Inbound Deliveries

Purchasing Document Category F + Order Type (Purchasing) ZNB2 + Plant 1310 + Storage Location 131C -> Confirmation Control Key 0004

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Logistics Execution -> Shipping -> Deliveries -> Define Order Confirmations for Inbound Deliveries

 

18 Set Up Confirmation Control

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Materials Management -> Purchasing -> Confirmations -> Set Up Confirmation Control

 

19 Define Internal Confirmation Categories

Confirmation Category(LA) -> Delivery Type(EL) + Delivery Type Inbound Delivery Stock in Transit(ELST)

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Materials Management -> Purchasing -> Confirmations -> Define Internal Confirmation Categories

 

20 Define Item Category Determination in Deliveries

Deliverty Type ELST + Item Category Group NORM + Usage V + Item category of the higher-level item(Blank) -> Item Category(ELST)

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Logistics Execution -> Shipping -> Deliveries -> Define Item Category Determination in Deliveries

System would read this configuration when creating the inbound delivery for the purchasing company (1310) after posting PGI for supplying company(1710).

 

21 Define Delivery Item Categories

IMG Menu Path: SAP Customizing Implementation Guide -> Logistics Execution -> Shipping -> Deliveries -> Define Delivery Item Categories

Movement type 109 is used when the receiving company (1310) posts goods receipt via tcode MIGO to transfer stock from valuated blocked stock to unrestricted stock. In this step, only a material document would be generated but not accounting document.

 

22. OMJJ Change Movement Type(Movement Type 685 -> GBB-VAY)

 

23. OKB9 Define Default Account Assignment(Activate PrfSeg for G/L Account corresponding to GBB-VAY)

 

Part C. Data Preparation:

Supplier IC1710(Under Receiving company code 1310)

Customer IC1310(Under Supplying company code 1710)

Material RM12 (Under Supplying company code 1710)

Material RM12 (Under Receiving company code 1710)

VK11 Create Condition Records for SD Tax Condition Type(UTXJ)

VV21 Create Output Condition Record(Condition Type SPED)

 

Part D. End to End Testing Records:

1.STO created by Receiving Company 1310

    2.Document Flow of Supplying Company 1710

3.Outbound Delivery 80000043 Created by Supplying Company 1710 through VL10B/VL10D wrt to STO

Click Extras -> Delivery Output -> Header to check the status of output type SPED

4.Accounting Document 4900000026 Corresponding to Material Document 4900000176

5.Inbound Delivery (of receiving Company 1310) created automatically when executing PGI for Outbound Delivery 80000043

6.Material Document 4900000177 created by Executing POD(VLPOD), the 1st line item is for Supplying Company 1710, and the 2nd one is for Receiving Company 1310, and 2 accounting documents generated respectively.

7.Accounting Document 4900000027(of Supplying Company 1710) Corresponding to 1st line item of Material Document 4900000177

Entry View

8.Accounting Document 4900000004 (of Receiving Company 1310) Corresponding to 2nd line item of Material Document 4900000177

9.Billing Document 90000053 of Supplying Company 1710

10.Accounting Document 9300000009 of Supplying Company 1710 corresponding to Billing Document 90000053

*Please note that for entry view the field Profit. Segment is greyed out.

 

General Ledger View

*In contrast to Entry view, we can see that for General Ledger view the field Profit. Segment is activated, which means General Ledger View data have been posted into CO-PA.

 

11.Goods Receipt WRT to Inbound Delivery 180000001

Movement Type 109 is used to transfer goods from Valuated blocked stock to Unrestricted stock, only material document generate by not accounting document.

12.MM Invoice (of Receiving Company 1310) 5105600123 generated by executing MIRO against STO 4500000030

Part D. Defects and Solutions

Defect 1:

Below 2 error messages raised for Output Type SPED after executing PGI for Outbound Delivery, PGI has been posted successfully though.

Message no. M7873 Movement type 101 is not allowed

Message no. /SPE/STO_HANDLING002 No inbound delivery created for the replenishment delivery 0080000044

Root Cause:

Field DelTyp SiT is blank for Confirmation Category LA in my case.

Solution:

Assign ELST (Populate it into Field DelTyp SiT) to Confirmation Category LA, and try to repeat Output again.

 

Defect 2:

Root Cause:

SAP would use movement type 685 to generate material document during VLPOD, hence to the G/L account (In our case 50100000) configured for GBB-VAX corresponding to movement type 658 would be posted, and as per settings of movement type 685 the indicator “Check acct.ass.” is activated(selected),  however the G/L Account Type of G/L account 50100000 is N Nonoperating Expense or Income.

entry.title: Re: Shortest code to demonstrate reload of dropdown in CL_GUI_ALV_GRID
entry.content:
The below code produces this output and button to reload dropdown lists:

REPORT zdemo.

PARAMETERS dummy.

CLASS lcl_app DEFINITION DEFERRED.
DATA app TYPE REF TO lcl_app.

AT SELECTION-SCREEN OUTPUT.
  IF app IS NOT BOUND.
    CREATE OBJECT app TYPE ('LCL_APP').
    CALL METHOD app->('PBO').
  ENDIF.

CLASS lcl_app DEFINITION.
  PUBLIC SECTION.
    METHODS pbo.

  PRIVATE SECTION.
    DATA alv              TYPE REF TO cl_gui_alv_grid.
    DATA table_of_flights TYPE TABLE OF sflight.

    METHODS on_toolbar FOR EVENT toolbar OF cl_gui_alv_grid
      IMPORTING e_object e_interactive.

    METHODS on_user_command
      FOR EVENT user_command OF cl_gui_alv_grid
      IMPORTING e_ucomm.

    METHODS reload_dropdown.
ENDCLASS.


CLASS lcl_app IMPLEMENTATION.
  METHOD pbo.
    SELECT * FROM sflight INTO TABLE table_of_flights.
    CREATE OBJECT alv
      EXPORTING i_parent = cl_gui_container=>screen0.

    SET HANDLER on_toolbar FOR alv.
    SET HANDLER on_user_command FOR alv.

    alv->set_drop_down_table( it_drop_down = VALUE #(
      ( handle = '1' value = 'A319' )
      ( handle = '1' value = 'A320-200' ) ) ).

    alv->set_table_for_first_display( EXPORTING i_structure_name = 'SFLIGHT'
                                                is_layout        = VALUE #( edit = 'X' )
                                      CHANGING  it_outtab        = table_of_flights ).
    alv->get_frontend_fieldcatalog( IMPORTING et_fieldcatalog = DATA(lt_fieldcatalog) ).
    lt_fieldcatalog[ fieldname = 'PLANETYPE' ]-drdn_hndl = 1.
    alv->set_frontend_fieldcatalog( lt_fieldcatalog ).
    alv->refresh_table_display( ).
  ENDMETHOD.

  METHOD on_toolbar.
    IF e_interactive = abap_false.
      " Added the first time only
      INSERT VALUE #( function = 'RELOAD_DROPDOWN'
                      text     = 'Reload dropdown' ) INTO e_object->mt_toolbar INDEX 1.
    ENDIF.
  ENDMETHOD.

  METHOD on_user_command.
    CASE e_ucomm.
      WHEN 'RELOAD_DROPDOWN'.
        reload_dropdown( ).
    ENDCASE.
  ENDMETHOD.

  METHOD reload_dropdown.
    alv->set_drop_down_table( it_drop_down = VALUE #(
        ( handle = '1' value = 'A380-800' )
        ( handle = '1' value = 'B747-400' ) ) ).
    alv->refresh_table_display( is_stable = VALUE #( row = 'X'
                                                     col = 'X' ) ).
  ENDMETHOD.
ENDCLASS.

Sandra

entry.title: The standalone app — exploring supplier recommendations with RAP + Fiori Elements
entry.content:
A custom SAP S/4HANA AI use case, built responsibly on SAP BTP + SAP AI Core.

Part 3 of 3 — "AI‑Guided Supplier Selection in SAP S/4HANA". Part 1: the in‑transaction assistant (ME51N). Part 2: the SAP BTP + AI Core "brain". This part: the standalone RAP + Fiori Elements app. (Prototype / proof‑of‑concept — a custom extension, not standard/embedded functionality. System IDs, hostnames and deployment IDs are masked.)

TL;DR

Same AI, different doorway. In Part 1 the SAP AI Core recommendation lived inside ME51N — the buyer's in‑flow surface. But sometimes you want to step back and explore with the AI: compare suppliers across a whole basket of materials, let the model reason about whether one vendor can cover everything (one PO) or not (several), and tune the sourcing strategy. That's what this standalone RAP + Fiori Elements app does — the same guarded‑LLM engine as Part 1 and Part 2, wrapped in an interactive UI. It's a managed, draft‑enabled business object exposed as an OData V4 UI service, with one action, RankSuppliers, that orchestrates the AI recommendation end to end.

ranked suppliers and the sourcing scenario for a basket of materials

Two surfaces, one engine

Part 1's ME51N assistant is about flow — you're creating a requisition and the best vendor should just be there. This app is about exploration — a buyer or category manager asks, "for these five materials, what's the smartest way to source them?" Same KPIs, same guarded LLM, same validation — but here the answer includes a sourcing scenario across materials, not just a per‑line default.

  ME51N assistant (Part 1) Standalone app (this part)

Mindsetin‑flow, one line at a timeexplore a whole basket
Triggertyping a material in the PRcreate a Run, add materials, press Rank Suppliers
OutputDesired Vendor default + top‑5 popupranked suppliers + COMMON/SPLIT sourcing
Built withclassic BAdIRAP (managed BO) + Fiori Elements

The run header shows the sourcing scenario; items show the ranked suppliers

Annotated object page of a recommendation run

How it works (technical deep‑dive)

From here on it's for the developers. If you're here for the concept, skip to “Wrapping up the series”.

The business object

It's a two‑level managed, draft‑enabled RAP BO:

  • Run (root) — one recommendation run: the consolidation preference, and after ranking, the scenario type, supplier count (= number of POs), coverage %, and AI status.
  • Item (child) — the materials in the run and, after ranking, each material's recommended supplier, reason, and confidence.

Interface CDS (ZI_VENDORREC_RUN / ZI_VENDORREC_ITEM) model the composition; projection CDS (ZC_VENDORREC_RUN / ZC_VENDORREC_ITEM) add the Fiori UI annotations; a service definition + OData V4 UI binding expose it to Fiori Elements. A material value help (ZI_VENDORREC_MAT_VH) gives an F4 that auto‑fills description/plant/group.

Managed draft BO exposed as an OData V4 UI service

One action does the orchestration

The whole recommendation is a single RAP action on the Run — RankSuppliers. Its handler reads the run's items, builds one candidate request per material (via the deterministic engine from Part 2), calls the service once for the whole run (so it can reason about consolidation), then writes the picks back onto the items and the scenario onto the header (handler trimmed for brevity):

METHOD rank_suppliers.
  " Deterministic engine (candidates/KPIs) + thin AI client (calls the BTP service)
  DATA(svc) = NEW zcl_vendorrec_service( ).
  DATA(ai)  = NEW zcl_vendorrec_ai_core( iv_destination = 'Z_VENDORREC_API' ).

  READ ENTITIES OF zi_vendorrec_run IN LOCAL MODE
    ENTITY Run FIELDS ( ConsolidationPref ) WITH CORRESPONDING #( keys ) RESULT DATA(lt_runs).

  LOOP AT lt_runs INTO DATA(ls_run).
    " read this run's materials
    READ ENTITIES OF zi_vendorrec_run IN LOCAL MODE
      ENTITY Run BY \_Item FIELDS ( Material ) WITH VALUE #( ( %tky = ls_run-%tky ) ) RESULT DATA(lt_items).

    " one candidate request per material (KPIs computed deterministically in ABAP)
    DATA lt_req TYPE zcl_vendorrec_ai_core=>tt_llm_request.
    CLEAR lt_req.
    LOOP AT lt_items INTO DATA(ls_item).
      APPEND svc->build_llm_request( iv_material = ls_item-Material ) TO lt_req.
    ENDLOOP.

    " one call for the whole run -> honors the consolidation preference (COMMON/SPLIT)
    DATA(res) = ai->get_recommendation( it_requests = lt_req
                                        iv_consolidation_preference = ls_run-ConsolidationPref ).

    " write the recommendation back onto each item …
    " … and the scenario summary (type, #POs, coverage, AI status) onto the run header
  ENDLOOP.
ENDMETHOD.

Two things to note: the deterministic KPIs are computed in ABAP (nothing sensitive leaves S/4), and the sourcing scenario is derived server‑side, not by the LLM — exactly the guardrails from Part 2, reused unchanged.

Why RAP here, but a BAdI in ME51N?

Different jobs, different tools. ME51N already exists and the buyer is in it — enhancing it with a BAdI is the least‑intrusive way to add a default. This app is a new object with its own persistence, draft handling, and UI — which is exactly what RAP + Fiori Elements gives you almost for free (draft, locking, OData, List Report/Object Page). Same engine underneath; the right delivery vehicle for each context.

Consolidation preference: the buyer's strategy lever

The Run header carries a consolidation preference dropdown — CONSOLIDATE, BALANCED, BEST_FIT — which flows into the service call and steers the COMMON‑vs‑SPLIT decision (see Part 2). It's the one knob that lets a human set sourcing strategy while the AI does the reasoning: e.g. "prefer one supplier for the whole basket even at a small KPI cost," vs "give me the strongest supplier per material regardless."



Consolidation preference dropdown and the resulting sourcing scenario

Wrapping up the series

Across three parts we built one idea two ways, on one trustworthy engine:

  • Part 1 — ME51N: the recommendation in flow, defaulted into Desired Vendor with an explainable popup, via a supported BAdI.
  • Part 2 — BTP + AI Core: the guarded brain — deterministic KPIs in ABAP, an LLM kept honest by server‑side validation, secure S/4→BTP→AI Core connectivity, and no data leaving S/4 beyond KPIs.
  • Part 3 — RAP + Fiori: the explore surface — a managed draft BO that ranks suppliers across a basket and proposes the sourcing scenario.

The throughline is responsible, custom S/4HANA AI: deterministic where it must be, AI where it adds value, explainable and human‑in‑the‑loop throughout — built on SAP's own AI platform.

Where next? Extending the same pattern to purchase orders (ME21N), adding a price dimension, and turning the decision log into an adoption dashboard are the obvious next steps.

Thanks for reading the series. If you build something with this pattern — or take it somewhere we didn't — we'd genuinely like to hear about it in the comments.

entry.title: SAP Ariba Supplier Management & Risk 2611 Release Highlights
entry.content:
Hello SAP Ariba Supplier Management & Risk Community, 

Let's take a look at some of the features included in the Q4 2026 release for SAP Ariba Supplier Lifecycle & Performance and SAP Ariba Supplier Risk solutions. 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

 

SAP Ariba Supplier Lifecycle & Performance

Dimension-Based Filters for Supplier Evaluations [NGSM-3344]

This feature offers expanded filtering capabilities across supplier evaluation screens to help you find relevant evaluations more efficiently. You can now filter results using dimensions such as Geographical Region, Product Classification, Company Code, and other available dimensions. These new filters are available on key evaluation pages, making it easier to narrow down participants, questionnaires, and evaluation programs based on the dimensions most relevant to your organization.


Supplier Performance Evaluations: Add Participants to Programs in In-Progress and No-Response Status [NGSM-3350]

You can now add internal participants to an evaluation program and assign suppliers to them while the program cycle is in In Progress or No Response status. Previously, participants could only be added during program creation, before the cycle started. With this enhancement, program owners and program creators can add new participants and assign suppliers to them directly from the program detail page, even after the evaluation cycle has begun. A record of each change—including the user who made it, the timestamp, and the details of the change—is logged and displayed in the application.


Action Plan Management Integration with Supplier Profile [NGSM-3467]

You can now access and manage action plans from multiple entry points in the SAP Ariba Supplier Lifecycle and Performance interface, including the Manage menu and the supplier profile.


Supplier Questionnaire: Flexible Mapping in Scorecard [NGSM-3471]

You can now assign different sets of suppliers to individual questionnaires within a single evaluation program. Previously, all suppliers had to be mapped to every questionnaire before the program could be submitted. With this enhancement, you can independently map any subset of suppliers to each questionnaire, enabling multi-region assessments within one program; for example, mapping region-specific suppliers to separate regional questionnaires. The program can be submitted as long as each questionnaire has at least one supplier assigned.


Ability to Update ERP Vendor IDs for Integrated Suppliers Using Data Import [SLP-2349]

This feature adds the ability to use the Suppliers data import task in SM Administration to update ERP vendor IDs for integrated supplies. Previously, it was only possible to update ERP vendor IDs for suppliers with Not Integrated or In Process integration status or suppliers whose initial synchronization to the ERP system was in an error state using this data import.


Support for Flex Master Data in Supplier Management Questionnaires [SLP-2413]

This feature adds the ability to questions based on custom flex master data in supplier management questionnaires. You can use existing flex master data features to create custom data structures for storing master data specific to your organization, then add questions related to that data to supplier requests or registration questionnaires. Questionnaire respondents choose from flex master data values when adding answers.


Support for Setting Modular Questionnaire Project-Level Status to Archived for Archived Risk Assessments [SLP-2430]

This feature adds support for setting the project-level status of modular questionnaires archived as part of an engagement risk assessment project where they're included as risk assessments to Archived status. Setting these projects to Archived status at the project level means that all of their data remains available, approval graphs are never reset, and a clear audit trail of project activity is maintained.


Ability to Mass Cancel In-Progress Supplier Registration Projects [SLP-2456]

This feature adds the ability to mass cancel supplier registration projects with a registration status of *Invited*, *In Registration*, *Pending Approval*, or *Pending Resubmit*. Administrators use a data import task to specify the suppliers with registration projects in these statuses to cancel in a single operation. Previously, it was only possible to cancel registration projects individually using a manual procedure.

 

SAP Ariba Supplier Risk

Ability to View and Navigate to the Associated Engagement Request from the Contract Workspace [SRISK-1891]

This feature enables you to navigate directly from a Contract Workspace to its associated Engagement Request (ER) in Supplier Risk through a clickable Engagement Request ID link. The link opens the ER at the exact page where it was last left, and Go back to contract banner allows you to return seamlessly to the originating contract. You can review and edit the ER as permitted, completing contract and risk reviews in one continuous workflow.


Ability to Export Engagement List Status in English Across All Locales [SRISK-1900]

This feature enables you to export the engagement list with the *Status* column including phase name and status label in English, regardless of the locale in which the engagement request was created or the user's locale.


Ability to Execute Bulk Template Upgrades for Selected Engagement Requests [SRISK-1908]

This feature enables you to upgrade multiple selected engagement requests to a newer template version in a single bulk operation, eliminating the need to upgrade each engagement individually. Template upgrade enables you to update existing control-based engagement risk assessment projects to the latest published version of the supplier risk engagement template, ensuring your engagements always reflect your organization's most recent risk processes.

 

 Looking for more detailed information on a feature? If so, once these features are officially released (November 13th) you can locate additional implementation and technical details, by simply searching for the feature ID here: What's New (via SAP Help Portal)

 

Stay tuned for our additional upcoming blog posts and follow me to stay informed on upcoming feature releases across SAP Ariba.

​Thank you for being a part of the SAP Ariba community and we look forward to continuing our innovative journey together!

entry.title: MCP and SAP Integration Part 4: Who Gets to Act?
entry.content:
Introduction

The first time my AI agent tried to create a sales order in SAP S/4HANA, my own server stopped it:

NOT_AUTHORIZED: This client is not allowed to run prepare_sales_order.Required scope: Orders.Write.

That refusal was the best result of the whole series.

Here is why. Until now, my agent could only read : customers, sales orders, delivery status .If it got something wrong, the worst case was a wrong answer. The moment an agent can write , a mistake becomes an order for 500 pumps instead of 50, or the same order twice because a request was retried. A reader put it perfectly in a comment on Part 1: "Tool availability should never be confused with execution authority." An agent that can find a tool should not automatically be allowed to use it. 

So in this post, I let the agent create its first sales order, but only after it gets past four checks. By the end, you will see it get refused, ask a human for permission, create the order, and prove that it really happened:

  1. A locked back door: The server validates the XSUAA token itself.
  2. Execution authority: Separate Read and Write scopes, checked for every tool.
  3. A human in the loop: A preview first, and the real action only after the user says yes.
  4. Proof and traceability: The result is read back, a retry never creates a duplicate, and every tool call leaves an audit line.

End-to-End Security Overview 

A request to create a sales order now passes four checks. Each one can stop it, and each stop is a clear, non-retryable answer the agent can explain.

Checks 2, 3 and 4 run in the MCP server, because only the server sees which tool is called. Every tool call there leaves one audit line.

Step 1: Lock the back door : 

Part 3 found a gap: the Cloud Foundry URL of the MCP server answered without any key or token. Anyone who found it could skip SAP API Management and read live S/4HANAdata. Before adding a write tool, that door had to close.

The fix: The MCP server validates the XSUAA token itself , with SAP's library @SAP/xssec. It checks the signature, issuer, expiry and audience: the same check theVerifyJWT policy does in API Management, now also inside the server. 

  • Bind the existing XSUAA instance to the app in manifest.yml 
services: - mcp-destination - mcp-xsuaa​
  • Install the library:
npm install @SAP/xssec​
  • Check every /mcp call before it reaches the MCP SDK:
async function authenticate(req) { try { const ctx = await createSecurityContext(authService, { req }); const t = ctx.token; return { ok: true, info: { clientId: t.clientId, scopes: t.scopes || [] } }; } catch (e) { return { ok: false, status: 401, error: "Unauthorized: a valid XSUAA token is required" }; }}​
  • /health stays open, because Cloud Foundry needs it. On Cloud Foundry, a missing XSUAA binding never means "open": the server refuses every call with 503 instead.

The Result 

Step 2: Who may run which tool 

A valid token proves who is calling. It says nothing about what the caller may do. Until now, the token carried only one scope, uaa.resource .

Why the check belongs in the MCP server. MCP sends every tool call as a POST to the same /mcp endpoint, and the tool name sits inside the JSON body. API Management sees who is calling. Only the MCP server sees which tool is being called.

  • Define two scopes in xs-security.json : The client gets only Read for now: 
{ "xsappname": "<your xsappname, without the !t... part>", "tenant-mode": "shared", "scopes": [ { "name": "$XSAPPNAME.Orders.Read", "description": "Read customers and sales orders" }, { "name": "$XSAPPNAME.Orders.Write", "description": "Prepare and create sales orders" } ], "authorities": [ "$XSAPPNAME.Orders.Read" ]}​
cf update-service mcp-xsuaa -c xs-security.json

authorities decides which scopes the client-credentials token receives. The xsappnamemust match your existing instance:
cf env <app> shows it once XSUAA is bound.

  • My first attempt failed with "Cannot change tenant mode with update… from shared to dedicated". The tenant mode is fixed when the XSUAA instance is created, so check it before writing the file.
  • Check the token : A new token now carries the scope :
uaa.resourcena-63002c5d-...!t718802.Orders.Read​

  • Every tool declares its scope, and one check runs before any tool:
const scope = tool.scope || "Orders.Read";if (!hasScope(extra?.authInfo, scope)) { return toolError({ error: "NOT_AUTHORIZED", retryable: false, message: `This client is not allowed to run ${tool.name}. Required scope: ${scope}.` });}​

Read tools need Orders.Read. The new write tools, prepare_sales_order and confirm_sales_order , need Orders.Write .

The result: visible, but not allowed : 

With a Read-only token, I asked Cline:

"Create a sales order for customer 17100001: 3 pieces of material TG13".

Cline found prepare_sales_order in the tool list and called it. The server refused:

{ "error": "NOT_AUTHORIZED", "retryable": false, "message": "This client is not allowed to run prepare_sales_order. Required scope: Orders.Write."}

Cline explained it clearly: the connection can read orders but not create them, and "no order was created, the preparation step was blocked before anything happened." Because of retryable: false , it did not try again.

The server's own log shows who said no: ERR Tool prepare_sales_order refused: client sb-na-63002c5d-...!t718802 lacks scope Orders.Write .

The tool is available, but the agent has no authority to run it.

Cline suggested asking the "SAP API Management administrator" for the missing permission. That is slightly off, because the scope lives in XSUAA. The server decides; the agent only explains, and its explanation is a guess based on the error text. 

Step 3: A human in the loop : 

With Orders.Write added to authorities (and one more cf update-service), the client may create orders. But an agent that may write should still not write on its own. So creating an order takes two tools: 

The server alone cannot prove that a human said yes: The model could call confirm_sales_order by itself. So the human check has two layers on the client side as well:

  • Cline asks before every tool call : In Cline, under Auto-approve, untick Use MCP servers.
  • A rule in .clinerules :
## Creating sales orders- To create a sales order, first call prepare_sales_order and show the preview to the user.- Never call confirm_sales_order unless the user has seen that preview and replied "yes" in this conversation.- After confirm_sales_order, report the order number, status and whether it was verified. If the mode is "simulated", say so.​

The flow in Cline. I asked for the same order again. Cline returned a preview: customer17100001 (Domestic US Customer 1), material TG13, 3 PC, sales area 1710 / 10 / 00, order type OR. It added: "Nothing has been created yet. Do you confirm? Please reply yes."

Only after I typed yes did Cline call confirm_sales_order.

The rules guide the agent. The server enforces.

What confirms the business outcome?: 

An HTTP 201 proves that a request was accepted. It does not prove that the order exists in the state the user asked for. So
confirm_sales_order never answers from the POST response alone. After creating the order, it reads the order back and returns what the system actually holds, plus verified: true : 

{ "salesOrder": "SIM0000001", "customer": "17100001", "material": "TG13", "quantity": "3 PC", "status": "Open", "verified": true, "mode": "simulated - the SAP Business Accelerator Hub sandbox does not save new orders"}

Cline answered from that verified result:
"The sales order has been created: SIM0000001,customer 17100001, TG13, 3 PC, status Open, verified: yes."

Let's take one example here : When the server sends a create request (a POST) to SAP, SAP answers with a status code. 201 = “Created”, which basically means “I received your request and accepted it.”

“Accepted” is not the same as “exactly what you asked for”. It’s like ordering food: the waiter says “Order received!” (that’s the 201), but you only know your order is right when the plate arrives and you check it. Between the request and the result, things can differ:

  • SAP may fill in default values you didn’t send.
  • A field may be ignored or changed.
  • An item may be missing, or the order may be blocked later.

If the agent tells the user “Done!” based only on the 201, it may be reporting something that isn’t true.

Cline built its answer from the verified read-back, not from the request. So the user sees what the system really holds: order SIM0000001, customer 17100001, TG13, 3 PC, status Open, verified: yes.

Stated honestly: this order is simulated : The Business Accelerator Hub sandbox does not save new orders, so on the sandbox the write runs in a clearly labelled simulated mode, and Cline said so in its answer. With WRITE_MODE: live and the destination pointing to areal S/4HANA system, the same code does a real POST to A_SalesOrder (the SAP Cloud SDK fetches the CSRF token) and reads the new order back through the same API.

"Done" is a claim. "Verified" is a fact read back from the system. 

Retries without duplicates : 

In Part 3, a wrong retryable flag made the agent repeat a broken read six times. For reads that is annoying. For writes it is  dangerous: a retried "create" can mean two orders. So confirm_sales_order is idempotent. The server remembers the result for each confirmation Id . A second confirm with the same ID returns the first result and creates nothing.

I tested it by asking Cline: "Please confirm that order again."
The answer: "Confirmed, it's the same order, no duplicate was created: SIM0000001. Note: Already created earlier, no second order was created."

The other confirm cases are refused just as clearly:

All of them are marked retryable: false, so the agent stops and explains instead of looping.

Traceability: who called what, when, and what happened : 

In Part 1, I asked how an integration team would answer these questions once AI agentscall SAP: Which agent made the request? Which tool did it use? Where did it fail? How long did it take? Part 4 answers them with one audit line per tool call
.

  • API Management creates the ID: An Assign Message policy, the first step in Proxy Endpoint Pre Flow, adds a correlation ID to every request:
<AssignMessage async="false" continueOnError="false" enabled="true" xmlns="http://www.sap.com/apimgmt"> <Add> <Headers> <Header name="X-Correlation-ID">{messageid}</Header> </Headers> </Add> <IgnoreUnresolvedVariables>true</IgnoreUnresolvedVariables> <AssignTo createNew="false" type="request"/></AssignMessage>

The Debug Viewer shows it on the request sent to the MCP server, for example X-Correlation-ID: us10-trial-nonasg-router2-1054008-1330786-2.

 

  • The MCP server writes one AUDIT line per tool call : with that ID, the client, the tool, therequired scope, the decision and the outcome:
AUDIT {"correlationId":"...","client":"sb-na-...!t718802","tool":"get_order_updates","scope":"Orders.Read","decision":"allowed","outcome":"ok","ms":814}AUDIT {"correlationId":"...","client":"sb-na-...!t718802","tool":"prepare_sales_order","scope":"Orders.Write","decision":"allowed","outcome":"ok","ms":441}AUDIT {"correlationId":"...","client":"sb-na-...!t718802","tool":"confirm_sales_order","scope":"Orders.Write","decision":"allowed","outcome":"created SIM0000001","ms":1}

A refused call gets a line too, with "decision" :"refused" and "outcome":"NOT_AUTHORIZED"

To follow one request from the gateway to the server, take the ID from the Debug Viewer and search for it:

cf logs sap-mcp-server --recent | Select-String "<correlation id>"

"One request, one ID, from the gateway to the server log."

The reader's questions, answered : 

Tool availability is not execution authority. Now it is not just a principle, it is a check that runs on every call.

Wrapping Up : 

Over four posts, the same MCP server went from an idea, to a secured gateway, to live S/4HANA data, and now to an agent that may act, but only within clear limits. Cline, SAP API Management and the questions never changed. What changed is who may do what, and how we know what happened.
What I learned in this part:

  • A gateway needs a locked back door: The server must validate the token itself.
  • Authorization belongs where the tool name is visible: API Management knows who is calling; only the MCP server knows which tool.
  • Permissions can change without code: Moving from Read to Read and Write was one line in xs-security.json.
  • Split every write into prepare and confirm: The preview costs one extra message and buys a human decision.
  • Make writes safe to retry: The same confirmation must never create a second order.
  • Log every decision with one ID: It turns "what did the agent do?" into a search.

Discovery opens the door. Authorization decides who acts. Verification proves it happened.

Thank you to the reader whose comment on Part 1 turned this series into something much more useful than I first planned.

entry.title: Teaching an LLM to Speak ABAP: Lessons from an MCP Server
entry.content:
Note: This is a personal blog about two personal projects: the MCP server and the local Qwen model. The projects, the measurements, and the opinions in this blog are personal. They do not show the position of SAP SE.

Introduction

AI agents can now read, change, check, and activate ABAP code. They do this through MCP servers. An MCP server gives the agent a set of tools. Each tool sends requests to the ABAP system through the ADT REST interface.

The server in this blog is the EPOD ABAP MCP Server. It runs inside Eclipse ADT, or as a standalone server next to ADT for VS Code.

This blog shows the results of measurements: how agents use the tools, and what makes them use the tools well. The last section asks for your ideas.

A local ABAP model

A local ABAP model is also in progress: an open-weight Qwen model with 27B parameters, fine-tuned (supervised fine-tuning) for agent work with these tools. The model runs without a cloud service.

The training data comes from runs of large models on the same tools (teacher runs). Four rules for this data:

  • Do not remove calls from a teacher run. Later steps depend on them.
  • For each task, use the shortest successful run.
  • Remove repeats: the same tool with the same arguments, and calls with no use, for example an ATC run after a check that already said "ok".
  • After a change in the tool results, make the teacher runs again. The training data must show the same result shapes as the server.

The local model is also a good test for the tools. It shows problems that large models hide (Lesson 3).

Lesson 1: Measure where the tokens go

The basis is one ABAP read task with Claude Opus, with the cost read from the proxy dashboard. This is the distribution:

Item Share of cost

What a tool returns (written into the context cache)63%
The context, read again on each call29%
Output of the model4%
Input: prompt, instruction files, tool descriptions3%

Two rules come from this table:

  1. The size of a tool result is the largest cost. Return only the part that the agent needs.
  2. The number of calls is the second cost. Each extra call reads the full context again. One avoided call saves approximately 22 000 tokens in a typical session.

Examples from the measurements:

  • One method: approximately 500 tokens. The full class: approximately 25 000 tokens.
  • Three messages of a message class: 212 bytes. The full message class: 611 KB.
  • One edit cycle went from five calls to one call.

Lesson 2: The unit of change in ABAP is the method, not the line

Many coding agents edit files with an exact text replacement: "find this text, put that text". This works well for files. For ABAP, it causes problems.

A typical change: a call to a new method. In real code, this change also needs:

  • A variable for the result. In classic style, the DATA statement is at the start of the method, far from the call.
  • Error handling: TRY ... CATCH around the call, or RAISING in the method definition.
  • Changes in the lines that use the result.
  • The new method itself: its definition and its implementation.

The change is in several places. With text replacement, the agent must find a unique text for each place. ABAP repeats many lines (ENDIF., ENDMETHOD., CLEAR lv_x.), so the unique text gets longer. At the end, the agent sends almost the full method, with more risk and more calls.

ABAP developers think in objects, methods, and sections. The tools in this blog do the same. The agent asks for "method CALCULATE of class ZCL_X". The tool returns only this method. The agent writes the full method back in one call. The same call activates the object and reads the result again to confirm it.

Lesson 3: The shape of a tool result can make a model loop

After one release of the server, the local model started to loop. It sent the same two calls 9 to 26 times, in 4 of 11 tasks.

The result format caused the loops. For small classes, the method read returned JSON with the full class as one escaped string (\r\n in the text). Large models ignored this. The local model did not know this shape from its training.

The fix had two parts:

  • A tool result that contains ABAP source is plain text.
  • The shape of the result does not change with the size of the object. The model decides what it reads.

The loops stopped. The cost of the test scenarios went down by 3.4%. Unit tests now lock the result format, so a release cannot change it without notice.

Large models can hide such problems. A test with a small model shows them.

Lesson 4: Write tool descriptions like code, and test them

A tool description is the only manual that the model reads. Each description gets a test in a new session, without instruction files, with at least two clients (Claude Code and Codex CLI).

Three rules came from these tests:

  1. A description must work alone. Do not expect an AGENTS.md file to explain the tool.
  2. A description states facts. A sentence like "call tool X after this tool" made models call tool X when it had no use. Now the result says what the state is, and names the tool.
  3. A parameter text states the form and the effect. An error message is only the safety net.

In one test with 10 scenarios, better descriptions changed the result from 8 to 10 passed scenarios. The number of calls went from 18 to 15. For the dictionary objects (data elements, domains, table types), the pass rate went from 2 of 16 to 12 of 12.

Lesson 5: Eclipse ADT is the specification

The first tests ran on a new system. Then the tools ran on older releases. Some object creations and some activations failed.

For the fix, each request was compared with the request that Eclipse ADT sends for the same action: URI, parameters, media types, headers, body, and the next step after the response. Where Eclipse first reads system information (for example the discovery document), the server now reads the same information.

After this change, the defects stopped. Eclipse ADT works with all these releases, so the same requests work too.

Lesson 6: A green build proves nothing about an ADT contract

Live tests on a real system found all contract defects. Unit tests found none of them. For this reason, the gate for each change is a live test.

Two more rules came from real defects:

  • Report success only when the system confirms it. After a write, the tool reads the object again and compares the values.
  • HTTP 404 means that the object is missing. All other errors name the system and the status.

Other features of the server

The server works together with the tools that SAP ships. Its focus is on work that goes beyond one object in one system:

  • Version history and the difference between versions.
  • Compare an object across systems.
  • Transport requests: list, release, and find the request of an object.
  • Where-used lists.
  • Short dumps: list, group, and analyze the cause.
  • Full support for dictionary objects.
  • A read-only mode for each system.

Get the server

  • Project page with installation steps: EPOD ABAP MCP Server update site
  • Eclipse update site URL (Help > Install New Software): https://git.epod.dev/erhan/epod-adt-mcp-updatesite/raw/branch/main/

Your ideas

The aim of this blog is to collect ideas from the community:

  • Which ABAP tasks do you give to an agent today?
  • Where does your agent waste calls or tokens with ABAP?
  • Which result format works best for your model?
  • Do you test your tools with small models? What did you find?

Write your ideas in the comments.

entry.title: Debugging External Hooks and Autoflow in SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2
entry.content:
Debugging External Hooks and Autoflow in SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2

This is the fifth article in a series on extensibility in SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2. This one covers what to do when something does not work.

Series so far:

  1. How to Update a Field in SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2: Three Ways to Get There
  2. Online Validation in SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2: Validation Rule or External Hook?
  3. Triggering Background Processes with Autoflow
  4. Testing Webhooks in SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2 Locally, Without Touching BTP
  5. Debugging External Hooks and Autoflow (this article)

The first four articles in this series built and tested real extensibility scenarios end to end: a field that updates itself, a save that blocks on a compliance check, an approval flow that runs in the background, a local setup that lets all of it be tested without touching BTP. Along the way, a fair number of things broke, some by accident, some on purpose to see what the failure looked like. This article is not a chronological account of those failures. It is the diagnostic process that came out of them: where to look first and which tool answers which question.

It also covers the two details that took longest to pin down: why a breakpoint can stop your code while SAP's save transaction still times out, and how to make that timeout stop mattering during debugging.

The Errors SAP Actually Shows You

A catalog of the exact error messages encountered in this series, what caused each one, and how to tell them apart.

  • Custom logic service is unavailable — appeared in my tests when a PreHook/PostHook returned an empty or unusable response (article 1)
  • HTTP 404 status code returned from external system for external pre-hook — wrong script/path listening (article 4)
  • Missing If Match tag (428) — PATCH sent without a valid If-Match header, part of Autoflow's write-back (article 3)
  • 9073: FAILED_PRECONDITION ... timed out — a hook did not respond within the timeout. Confirmed in this series from two unrelated causes: the self-deadlock case (article 4), and simply pausing too long on a breakpoint during a live debugging session (this article)
  • Cannot parse outbound synchronous message response. The expected content type for message response is application/json. — appears in Logs, not the UI. Its exact trigger was not confirmed in this series: deliberately sending the wrong Content-Type did not reproduce it, so treat this one as a lead, not a confirmed cause, until reproduced on purpose
  • Data has been modified. Please refresh and try again. — concurrency conflict on etag/If-Match during Autoflow's write-back, including the case of a human editing the same record an Autoflow is also updating

Where to Look First

Two sources, and they answer different questions.

ngrok's Web Inspector (127.0.0.1:4040), already introduced in the fourth article, shows what actually arrived at your machine and what you sent back. It is the ground truth for the wire: headers, raw body, everything, kept for every request, not just the last one.

The Logs tab in Extensibility Administration (next to External Hooks, Determinations, and Validations in SAP's own UI) shows what SAP itself concluded from the exchange, in its own words. This is not redundant with the Inspector. A real example from this series: a historical entry read Error raised from the connector service for external hook 'Prehook_Custom_field': Cannot parse outbound synchronous message response. The expected content type for message response is application/json. That sentence names the hook, the exact failure category, and a plausible cause, information ngrok has no way to produce, since it never sees how SAP interpreted the response, only what was sent.

 Two things worth knowing about this tab before relying on it:

  • In the entries inspected during this series, the Logs tab appeared to record failures rather than successful executions. Across nine entries checked, every one was an ERROR; none was a confirmation of a clean run.
  • Not every error message it produces should be trusted as a precise diagnosis on the first read. Deliberately sending a wrong Content-Type (text/plain instead of application/json) to reproduce the message above did not reproduce it, the same hook processed the response and updated the field normally. The historical error's real cause remains unconfirmed. Logs tells you what SAP concluded, not necessarily the one true cause, and a message worth investigating is not the same as a message worth quoting as fact until it has been reproduced on purpose.

What Logs reproduced cleanly, on the other hand, deliberately and predictably, is a timeout, covered next.

Your Debugging Toolkit: VS Code and ngrok's Replay

Two tools do most of the work once something has already gone wrong once: VS Code's debugger, for stepping through your own code, and ngrok's Replay button, for re-sending a real captured request without going back into SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2 and saving a record again.

VS Code setup. The one fix that mattered: launch through Run → Python Debugger: Debug Python File (or F5, with the target file active), never by typing the run command directly into a terminal. A script started in a plain terminal executes normally but ignores every breakpoint silently, no error to point at the mistake. Once launched correctly, a breakpoint inside a module imported by the dispatcher stops execution exactly where set, real payload values visible in the Variables panel. That is the method used throughout this series; a more elaborate launch.json setup was not needed to get there.

 ngrok's Replay. Covered briefly in the fourth article, this deserves more detail here specifically as a debugging tool. Once a request has been captured, in the Inspector, opening it and clicking Replay resends the exact same payload to your currently running server, no SAP save required.

That original request completed in 7.04ms, unremarkable on its own. What makes Replay genuinely useful for debugging is what happens when you deliberately slow it down. Capturing that same request and replaying it, then holding a breakpoint inside the handler for over a minute before continuing, the same kind of pause that produces a timeout when the call is live and SAP is waiting, covered next, completed normally, HTTP 200, this time with a duration of 82.62 seconds shown directly in the Inspector.

The reason is straightforward once stated: the original request came from SAP, and SAP was the one enforcing the timeout while waiting for a response. The replayed request does not come from SAP at all, ngrok is the caller this time, resending the same bytes to the local server directly. There is no SAP save transaction on the other end waiting for anything, so SAP's synchronous External Hook timeout is no longer part of the debugging loop. This turns the debugging loop from "change code, save a quote, wait, check the result" into "change code, click Replay, check the result", and it is the natural complement to setting a breakpoint: capture the problematic request once, then Replay it as many times as needed while adjusting code and breakpoints, without putting the original SAP save transaction back into the debugging loop.

Finding Where the Failure Is

Three questions, asked in order, cover every failure encountered in this series:

Did the request reach ngrok? Check the Web Inspector first, it keeps a full history, not just the last attempt. Nothing arriving at all points at SAP-side configuration, not at your code: the Communication System host, whether the API Path or Subscribe Path matches what the External Hook or Autoflow rule actually points to, or whether the hook is even active. This is also where the one Pre plus one Post limit per entity shows up, as a configuration-time block rather than a runtime error, worth knowing about even though its full story belongs in a future article.

Did SAP accept the HTTP exchange? If the request did arrive, the next question is whether SAP was able to make sense of what came back, or of the exchange itself. HTTP 404 status code returned from external system for external pre-hook means the wrong script was listening on the path SAP called. Custom logic service is unavailable appeared in my tests when the hook returned an empty response instead of the expected response contract. 9073: FAILED_PRECONDITION ... timed out means SAP gave up waiting, whether because nothing responded at all or because something, a deadlock, a paused breakpoint, kept the answer from arriving in time. None of these say anything about whether your own logic was correct, only that the exchange itself did not complete the way SAP expects it to.

Did your code produce the expected result? Once the exchange itself is clean, an accepted request with a well-formed response, the remaining question is purely about logic: did the handler compute the right thing from the payload it received. This is where re-triggering from SAP every time is the slow way to find out. A breakpoint, a Replay, or an offline run against a captured payload all answer this same question, each with a different amount of friction and a different relationship to SAP's own clock, as covered above.

Debugging Live Calls with Breakpoints

The launch method covered above, through VS Code's own debugger rather than a plain terminal, is what makes stopping on a breakpoint possible in the first place, whether the trigger is a live SAP save or a Replay. What differs between the two is what happens if you take your time once execution has stopped.

SAP's own timeout does not know or care that a debugger is involved: it keeps counting from the moment the request was sent, for as long as the connection stays open on its side. Pausing on a breakpoint for over a minute during a live PreHook call, then resuming, produced exactly the failure predicted by the platform's own limits:

External pre-hook 'Prehook_Custom_field' for sap.crm.salesquoteservice.entity.salesQuote timed out.

 

The debugger worked, and the save still failed, and neither contradicts the other: from SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2's side, ten seconds of silence looks the same whether the code is stuck, crashed, or simply paused on a line you are inspecting. A breakpoint on a live synchronous hook is fine for a quick look at a variable; it is the wrong tool for sitting and thinking. For that, Replay above removes SAP's clock from the equation entirely, and the offline alternative below removes the network as well.

The Offline Alternative: Replaying a Captured Payload

Since every handler in this series was refactored into a plain function (handle(body) in, response or nothing out, from the fourth article's dispatcher redesign), the fastest debugging loop does not involve SAP or ngrok at all: capture a real payload once, save it, then call the handler directly against it.

The payloads do not need to be invented or generated from SAP's own "Generate Sample Payload" feature. ngrok's Web Inspector, introduced in the fourth article, already recorded a real one. To capture it:

  1. Trigger a real call from SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2 (save the Sales Quote).
  2. In the Web Inspector, select the request (POST /API_Prehook_custom_field).
  3. Open the Raw tab and copy just the JSON body, exactly as SAP sent it.
  4. Save it, prehook_sales_quote.json in this case, the same file used earlier in this series to confirm which fields SAP includes in currentImage. The same technique applies to any other hook or event; capturing one is enough to show the pattern.

From there, the same handler design also makes offline testing straightforward, with no server, ngrok, or SAP involved:

import json
import prehook_custom_field

with open("payloads/prehook_sales_quote.json", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    body = json.load(f)

response = prehook_custom_field.handle(body)
print(response)

The real value shows up once you start editing the captured payload to provoke scenarios you have not seen naturally yet, without touching SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2 at all:

body["currentImage"]["totalValues"]["netAmount"]["content"] = 20000000
response = prehook_custom_field.handle(body)
print(response)

This gives a third debugging layer alongside the first two covered in this article: a real SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2 call, ngrok's Replay of a captured request, and a captured payload run directly against your own code with no network involved at all. The Web Inspector doubles as the recorder for that last layer's test data.

The Rule of Thumb

Start with the three questions above, in order: did the request arrive, did the exchange complete, did the logic produce the right result. Each one points at a different place to look, and answering them in that order avoids the most common waste of time in this area, debugging application logic for a request that never reached your endpoint in the first place.

Once the problem is narrowed down to "my code did the wrong thing," pick the tool by how much of SAP's own clock you can afford to ignore. A live breakpoint against a real SAP save is the most realistic test, and the most fragile, SAP's synchronous timeout keeps counting the whole time you are paused. Replay removes that specific pressure, the same payload, the same breakpoints, no save transaction waiting on the other end. An offline run against a captured payload removes the network entirely, no server, no SAP, no ngrok, just the handler and the data it needs to prove a point. None of the three is strictly better than the others; each earns its place depending on whether what you are testing is the whole exchange, or just the logic inside it.

The five articles so far have now covered not only how these extensibility mechanisms work, but also what happens when they do not. In the next article, I will look at Reference Fields Usage and a question that should come before building another External Hook: can the data needed by a Validation or Determination be brought into native custom logic without writing code?

How to Implement

  • Implement a custom enhancement/user exit in the outbound INVOIC02 IDoc generation process (e.g., EXIT_SAPLVEDF_002 or relevant BAdI).

Recommendation: Avoid a global change. Implement the negative sign logic only for the specific partners or countries that require it and perform end-to-end testing before transport to production.
