entry.title: Part 2 of 2 – Securing AI-Powered SAP Apps on SAP BTP: Single Sign-On and Role-Based Access with XSU
entry.content:
Overview

Part 1 of this series described how SAP S/4HANA data can be made available to AI clients through an MCP server running on SAP BTP. Once such data is exposed through a user interface, the application must meet the same security standards as any other access to SAP systems.

This article describes how a UI application on SAP BTP, Cloud Foundry runtime, authenticates users and enforces authorizations using two standard platform components:

  • Application router – the single entry point that handles user login and request forwarding.
  • SAP Authorization and Trust Management service (XSUAA) – the service that issues tokens and manages scopes, role templates and role collections.

The approach addresses three requirements:

  • Authentication: only users with a valid corporate identity can access the application.
  • Authorization: each user can access only the functions assigned to them.
  • Enforcement: authorization decisions are made on the server and cannot be bypassed in the browser.

Solution components

Component Responsibility

Identity provider (for example, SAP Cloud Identity Services connected to the corporate directory)Authenticates the user through corporate single sign-on.
XSUAAIssues a signed JSON Web Token (JWT) containing the user's scopes, based on the assigned role collections.
Application routerActs as the single public entry point. Redirects unauthenticated users to the login, maintains the user session and forwards requests to the application together with the token.
UI applicationValidates the token on every request and grants access only to the functions permitted by its scopes.

Users always access the application through the application router, and the application validates the token independently. This provides two separate layers of control.

Authentication flow

The following steps describe the first access of a user to the application:

  1. The browser requests the application through the application router. No session exists yet.
  2. The application router redirects the request to XSUAA, which delegates authentication to the configured identity provider.
  3. The user authenticates with the corporate login, typically through single sign-on.
  4. The identity provider confirms the user's identity to XSUAA. XSUAA determines the user's role collections and issues a JWT containing the corresponding scopes.
  5. The application router stores the token in its server-side session and returns the requested page. The browser receives only a session cookie.
  6. For each subsequent request, the application router attaches the token and forwards the request to the application.
  7. The application validates the token (signature, expiry and audience) and evaluates the scopes before processing the request.

 

Figure 1: Authentication flow. The highlighted arrows show where the token is transferred; it is exchanged only between server-side components.

When the session expires, the application router repeats the flow from step 2.

Authorization model

XSUAA separates the definition of permissions from their assignment through three levels:

Level Purpose Maintained by

ScopeA single permission that the application checksDeveloper, in xs-security.json
Role templateGroups one or more scopes into a functional roleDeveloper, in xs-security.json
Role collectionBundles roles for assignment to users or user groupsAdministrator, in the SAP BTP cockpit

The complete xs-security.json is shown in step 1 of the configuration below.

With this model, access is managed entirely in the SAP BTP cockpit. Granting or revoking access requires no code change and no redeployment. Assigning role collections to user groups from the identity provider, rather than to individual users, keeps access aligned with organizational changes automatically.

Configuration steps

The following examples use generic names (my-xsuaa, my-approuter, my-ui-app) and placeholders in angle brackets. Replace them with the values of your own subaccount.

Step 1: Define the security descriptor (xs-security.json)

{
  "xsappname": "my-ui-app",
  "tenant-mode": "dedicated",
  "scopes": [
    { "name": "$XSAPPNAME.Display", "description": "Use the application" },
    { "name": "$XSAPPNAME.Monitor", "description": "Use the monitoring functions" }
  ],
  "role-templates": [
    { "name": "Viewer",         "scope-references": ["$XSAPPNAME.Display"] },
    { "name": "MonitoringUser", "scope-references": ["$XSAPPNAME.Display", "$XSAPPNAME.Monitor"] }
  ],
  "role-collections": [
    { "name": "App Viewers",      "role-template-references": ["$XSAPPNAME.Viewer"] },
    { "name": "Monitoring Users", "role-template-references": ["$XSAPPNAME.MonitoringUser"] }
  ],
  "oauth2-configuration": {
    "redirect-uris": ["https://<approuter-host>.cfapps.<region>.hana.ondemand.com/**"]
  }
}

Create the XSUAA service instance from this file. Later changes are applied to the same instance with update-service:

cf create-service xsuaa application my-xsuaa -c xs-security.json
cf update-service my-xsuaa -c xs-security.json

Step 2: Configure the application router

The application router is a small Node.js application based on the @SAP/approuter package. It needs three files.

package.json:

{
  "name": "my-approuter",
  "dependencies": { "@sap/approuter": "^20" },
  "scripts": { "start": "node node_modules/@sap/approuter/approuter.js" }
}

xs-app.json – every route requires an XSUAA login, and requests are forwarded to the UI application:

{
  "welcomeFile": "/",
  "authenticationMethod": "route",
  "logout": { "logoutEndpoint": "/logout" },
  "routes": [
    {
      "source": "^/(.*)$",
      "target": "/$1",
      "destination": "ui-app",
      "authenticationType": "xsuaa",
      "csrfProtection": false
    }
  ]
}

manifest.yml – the destination ui-app points to the UI application, and forwardAuthToken passes the user's token on:

applications:
  - name: my-approuter
    memory: 256M
    services:
      - my-xsuaa
    env:
      destinations: >
        [ { "name": "ui-app",
            "url": "https://<ui-app-host>.cfapps.<region>.hana.ondemand.com",
            "forwardAuthToken": true } ]

Set csrfProtection according to your application. If the UI application implements its own CSRF protection, the router's protection can be switched off for its routes, as shown above.

Step 3: Bind XSUAA to the UI application

The UI application needs the same XSUAA instance to validate the tokens it receives. Add it to the application's manifest.yml:

applications:
  - name: my-ui-app
    services:
      - my-xsuaa

Deploy both applications:

cf push my-ui-app
cf push my-approuter

Step 4: Configure trust and assign roles

In the SAP BTP cockpit, open Security → Trust Configuration and establish trust with your identity provider. Then assign the role collections under Security → Role Collections, preferably to user groups. With the SAP BTP command line interface, the assignment can also be scripted:

btp assign security/role-collection "Monitoring Users" --to-user <user@example.com>

Server-side authorization checks

The application router ensures that only authenticated users reach the application. Fine-grained authorization is performed by the application itself, on the server, for every request:

  1. Validate the forwarded token and reject requests with a missing, expired or foreign token.
  2. Read the scopes from the token.
  3. Expose only the functions and data permitted by those scopes, both in the user interface and in the server's API responses.

Because these checks run on the server, they cannot be circumvented by modifying the page or by calling the application's API directly.

For Node.js applications, SAP provides the @SAP/xssec and @SAP/xsenv packages for token validation. A minimal example with Express:

const express = require("express");
const xsenv = require("@sap/xsenv");
const { XsuaaService, createSecurityContext } = require("@sap/xssec");

const xsuaa = new XsuaaService(xsenv.getServices({ xsuaa: { tag: "xsuaa" } }).xsuaa);
const app = express();

// 1. Validate the token on every request
app.use(async (req, res, next) => {
  try {
    req.authInfo = await createSecurityContext(xsuaa, { req });
    next();
  } catch (e) {
    res.status(401).json({ error: "Not authenticated" });
  }
});

// 2. Require a scope for a protected function
const requireScope = (scope) => (req, res, next) =>
  req.authInfo.checkLocalScope(scope) ? next() : res.status(403).json({ error: "Not authorized" });

app.get("/api/monitoring", requireScope("Monitor"), (req, res) => {
  res.json({ status: "ok" });   // only reached with the Monitor scope
});

app.listen(process.env.PORT || 8080);

For Java applications, the SAP Cloud Security Services Integration Library (java-security) offers the same functions.

Backend connectivity

User authentication protects access to the application. Communication between the application and SAP S/4HANA is a separate, technical connection through an SAP BTP destination and the SAP Cloud Connector, using a technical user. As a result, SAP S/4HANA authorizes the technical user rather than the individual end user.

This is suitable for a proof of concept. For productive use, principal propagation should be considered, so that the end user's own SAP authorizations are also applied in the backend system.

Handling session expiry in the UI

When the application router session expires, background requests (for example fetch calls) receive a login redirect or an HTTP 401 instead of data. A reload of the page lets the application router restart the authentication flow:

async function callApi(url, options) {
  const res = await fetch(url, { credentials: "include", ...options });
  const isJson = (res.headers.get("content-type") || "").includes("application/json");
  if (res.status === 401 || !isJson) {
    window.location.reload();        // the application router redirects to the login
    return null;
  }
  return res.json();
}

Key considerations

Topic Consideration

Role changesScopes are written into the token at login. After a role collection is assigned or removed, the user must log in again for the change to take effect.
Session expiryBackground requests cannot complete an interactive login. When a session expires, the application should reload the page so that the application router can restart the authentication flow.
Service updatesUpdates to the XSUAA instance must be applied with the intended xs-security.json. Verify the resulting roles in the SAP BTP cockpit after each update.
Client-side restrictionsHiding functions in the user interface does not replace server-side authorization checks.
CredentialsTechnical credentials, such as API keys, should be provided through service bindings rather than environment variables or source code.

Summary

The application router and XSUAA provide a UI application on SAP BTP with the same authentication and authorization model as any other SAP BTP application:

  • A single entry point with corporate single sign-on.
  • Permissions carried in a signed token, defined by developers and assigned by administrators.
  • Authorization decisions enforced on the server.

An application that exposes SAP data through AI therefore requires no dedicated security model; it integrates into the standard security concept of SAP BTP. Principal propagation is the logical next step to extend user-specific authorizations to the SAP backend.

entry.title: SAP Business Network for Logistics 2610 – What’s New?
entry.content:
The October 2026 release of SAP Business Network for Logistics brings a focused set of enhancements across both SAP Business Network Freight Collaboration and SAP Business Network Global Track and Trace. This post walks through the highlights — what's new, what it means for you, and where to find more detail.

Cross SAP Business Network Freight Collaboration and SAP Business Network Global Track and Trace

Feature enhancement for integration logs

The 'Manage Integration Log' app has been upgraded. You can switch to it by clicking the 'New Version' button in the upper right corner of the app.

The old version is deprecated with this release but remains available alongside the new one for several months, giving you time to make the transition at your own pace. The end-of-life date for the old version will be communicated once confirmed.

What's new in the app:

  • Improved search: new header search fields for ‘Document ID’, ‘Type Description’, ‘Scenario’, and ‘Correlation ID’ make it faster to find specific entries in high-volume environments.
  • Richer filtering: the header now includes ‘Overall Status’ and ‘Business Partner’ filters alongside the existing ‘Document ID’ and ‘Received On’ filters.
  • Built-in Analytics: a new ‘Analytics’ tab shows the volume and status of application message types — such as ‘TransportationOrderRequest’ for Freight Collaboration or ‘TrackedProcessAndEvent’ for Global Track and Trace — giving you an at-a-glance operational picture.

  •  Expanded exports: higher export limits reduce manual filtering and support complete dataset retrieval for audit, compliance, and operational reporting.
  • Clearer error handling: when you select multiple messages for reprocessing, error messages are now displayed individually per correlation ID in a more readable format — making troubleshooting significantly easier.

Why it matters: integration logs are central to managing the health of your network connections. The new analytics capability in particular turns the app from a reactive troubleshooting tool into a proactive monitoring dashboard. Higher export limits are especially valuable for customers running high transaction volumes who need complete datasets for compliance reporting.

2027 Release Schedule Now Available

The release schedule for 2027 is now published for both SAP Business Network Freight Collaboration and SAP Business Network Global Track and Trace. Planning ahead for system maintenance windows just got easier.

 

SAP Business Network Freight Collaboration

Action Required: Migrate to SAP Data Privacy Integration Next Generation Service

This one requires your attention. SAP Business Network Freight Collaboration is migrating from the Personal Data Manager to the Next Generation Data Privacy Integration service ahead of schedule (now October 17, 2026), requiring shippers to subscribe to the ngdpi plan and carriers to use the new Manage Personal Data app via a dedicated URL.

For shippers:

  1. In your SAP Cloud Platform subaccount, subscribe to the Data Privacy Integration Next Generation service (application plan name: `ngdpi`).
  2. Assign the `DPI_NextGen_Information_DataPrivacy_Administrator` role collection to users responsible for personal data management.

For full documentation, refer to Personal Data Record SAP Data Privacy Integration Next Generation Service on the SAP Help Portal.

For carriers:

You can use the ‘Manage Personal Data’ app of the Data Privacy Integration Next Generation service. The app is accessible at:

https://<your-subdomain>.app.<region(eu10/us20/us30)>.ngdpi.dpp.cloud.sap.

For more information, see Personal Data Record in the SAP Help Portal.

Why it matters: Staying on the current DPI service means relying on a deprecated integration path. Migrating to ngDPI ensures continued compliance with data privacy regulations and access to the latest capabilities for managing personal data records across your network.

 

Planning and Subcontracting Process Enhanced

This release brings several improvements to the freight subcontracting process, spanning API and EDI capabilities.

Product ID sharing via the Consumer API:

The ‘Consumer API for Freight Subcontracting’ now supports sharing the ‘Product ID’ with the carrier. This closes an information gap that previously required manual workarounds, enabling carriers to better plan and execute shipments for products requiring specific handling.

Richer date/time fields in the Provider API:

The ‘Provider API for Freight Subcontracting’ now exposes pickup start/end date and time as well as delivery start/end date and time as new fields. This gives carriers and logistics partners a much more precise picture of the time constraints associated with each leg of a subcontracted shipment — reducing misalignments and improving execution accuracy.

Star-shaped stage sequences in outsourced planning:

Outsourced planning for freight units now supports star-shaped and reverse star-shaped stage sequences — a common freight network topology where shipments converge to a hub before being distributed, or vice versa.

Notes and instructions via EDI 204:

It is now possible to share notes and instructions with carriers via EDI 204 using a new NTE node, supporting up to 20 segments. This expands the capacity to include additional notes or instructions in shipment EDI messages, which is useful for carriers and shippers exchanging richer data in complex multi-stop payloads

Why it matters: These enhancements collectively reduce friction in the subcontracting process. More data flowing between shippers and carriers via both API and EDI means fewer manual touchpoints, less room for misinterpretation, and ultimately better on-time performance.

Improved Booking Accuracy in Dock Appointment Scheduling

The ‘Manage Dock Appointments’ and ‘Self-Book Dock Appointments’ apps now display the ‘Location Description’ alongside the ‘Loading Point ID’ in edit mode, helping you make more accurate booking selections.

The location description is shown only when a location has been assigned to the loading point and a description was available at the time of the assignment.

Why it matters: A location description sounds like a small addition, but in practice it makes a real difference when multiple dock locations or warehouse areas share similar names. Displaying the description directly in booking details gives carriers and warehouse staff the context they need to arrive at the right location — reducing delays and misrouted arrivals.

 

SAP Business Network Global Track and Trace

Standard Extractor Enhancements: More Data Flowing from SAP S/4HANA

Three new data points are now transferred from SAP Transportation Management in SAP S/4HANA to SAP Business Network Global Track and Trace via the standard extractor:

  • Administrative audit data: ‘Created By/On’ and ‘Changed By/On’ fields are now included in the data transferred to GTT. This supports traceability and audit requirements by making it clear when a freight order or booking was created and who made changes — directly within the GTT visibility layer.
  • Container details: ‘Container ID’ and ‘Container type’ can now be sent to GTT via the container table. This information can be used for visibility providers to calculate carbon emissions. By default, the feature is disabled. You can enable it manually. For more information, see Send Containers Table to the GTT System.
  • Ordering party: The ‘Ordering Party’ for freight orders and bookings is now transferred to GTT. This supports more accurate downstream reporting and visibility, especially in complex multi-party logistics scenarios where the ordering party differs from the shipper.

For more information, see 3763702 

Why it matters: Better data in GTT means better visibility. Audit data supports compliance; container details unlock more accurate sustainability metrics; and the ordering party field closes an attribution gap in multi-party logistics flows. These are steady improvements to data completeness that pay dividends across reporting, compliance, and operational monitoring.

Improved Shipment Visibility: EDI 214 Carrier Tracking Numbers Now Visible

Carrier tracking numbers sent by carriers via EDI 214 (L11 segment) are now automatically visible in SAP Business Network Global Track and Trace.

A new mapping was added between two data points:

  • EDI side: The L11 segment with qualifier CI (Unique Consignment Identifier) — this is where carriers include their tracking number in an EDI message
  • API side: The carrierDocumentReference field in the POST /OrderEvents API — this is how GTT (Global Track and Trace) receives that tracking number

Why it matters: Previously, if a carrier sent a tracking number via EDI, it would not be passed through to GTT. Now it is — meaning the tracking number travels end-to-end from the carrier's EDI message all the way into SAP Business Network Global Track and Trace, giving shippers and logistics teams better shipment visibility without needing to look up tracking numbers elsewhere.

 

What's Coming Next: Join Our 2611 Webcast

Already curious about what comes after 2610? We are too — and we want to share it with you directly. On Wednesday, November 18, 2026, our product and development experts will walk you through the high-impact features arriving with the 2611 release of SAP Business Network for Logistics. You'll get first-hand insight into:

  • Outbound flow for e-Invoicing in SAP Business Network Freight Collaboration
  • Time-based notifications in SAP Business Network Global Track and Trace
  • Unified, adaptive company profile for carriers — available across both Freight Collaboration and Global Track and Trace

The session starts at 11:30 AM CET — the session will be recorded in case you cannot join at this time. Register now for the SAP Business Network for Logistics 2611 Webcast

 

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Where to learn more

For the complete feature list and technical details, refer to the SAP Business Network for Logistics documentation on SAP Help Portal.

As always, feel free to leave a comment below with any questions or feedback — or connect via the SAP Community.

entry.title: Calling SAP SuccessFactors from Postman with OAuth 2.0 (SAML Bearer Assertion) - No External Tools
entry.content:
SAP SuccessFactors is retiring HTTP Basic Authentication (user and password) for its APIs. The retirement is planned for November 2026, and published sources give either 13 or 20 November, so the earlier date is the safer one to plan for. After that date, OData calls and SOAP calls such as CompoundEmployee will only accept token-based authentication.

If you use SAP Integration Suite (CPI), the switch is mostly a matter of configuration: you create an OAuth2 SAML Bearer Assertion credential and the adapter handles the rest. Manual testing in Postman has no equivalent built-in support. This post explains how to reproduce, step by step, what CPI does internally, using only Postman and OpenSSL.

The complete Postman collection, with all scripts in English, is attached to this post.

What you will be able to do

  • Generate your own RSA key pair and X.509 certificate.
  • Register an OAuth 2.0 client application in SAP SuccessFactors.
  • Build and digitally sign a SAML 2.0 assertion inside Postman, without any external tool.
  • Exchange the assertion for an OAuth access token and call the OData API.
  • Open an SFAPI session with the token and query CompoundEmployee over SOAP.

No prior OAuth or SAML knowledge is assumed. The explanations cover what happens at each step and why.

How it works

The method is the OAuth 2.0 SAML Bearer Assertion grant. Instead of sending a password, you send SuccessFactors a short XML document, the assertion. The assertion states that the application with a given API Key is acting as a given user and that the request is valid for the next 10 minutes. You sign the assertion with a private key. SuccessFactors verifies the signature with the public certificate you registered earlier. If the signature matches, it returns an access token valid for about 24 hours, and you attach that token to every API call.

The setup has two parts:

  1. One-time setup: create a technical user with the right permissions, generate a key pair, register the certificate in an OAuth client in SuccessFactors, and create a Postman environment.
  2. Every session: generate the assertion, get the token, then call the OData API or open an SFAPI session and query CompoundEmployee.

Step A: Technical user and permissions

Create or reuse a dedicated technical user, for example API_TECH_USER, and assign a permission role that includes:

  • Employee Central API → Employee Central HRIS OData API and Foundation OData API, for access to Employee Central entities.
  • Employee Central API → Employee Central HRIS SOAP API, required for CompoundEmployee.
  • General User Permission → SFAPI User Login, required to open an SFAPI session.
  • The target population and field-level RBP. These define which employees and fields the API returns. If they are too narrow, you get empty results.

The permission Allow Admin to Access OData API through Basic Authentication is not needed for OAuth. Once the migration is complete, you can remove it to verify that nothing still depends on Basic Authentication.

Step B: Key pair and certificate

Generate a self-signed certificate and private key with OpenSSL:

openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -sha256 -days 36500 -nodes \
  -keyout private.pem -out cert.pem -subj "/CN=postman-sf-ACMECORPT1"

Key points:

  • -nodes leaves the private key unencrypted. The Postman script needs an unencrypted PKCS#8 key.
  • The validity period is a decision to make together with the customer, in line with their security policy. A long validity avoids renewing the certificate and updating every Postman environment each year. A shorter lifetime reduces the impact if the key leaks. Either way, record the expiry date with openssl x509 -in cert.pem -noout -enddate.

SuccessFactors and the Postman variables need the Base64 content without the BEGIN/END lines and without line breaks. On Linux, macOS or Git Bash:

grep -v -- "-----" private.pem | tr -d '\n' > private_b64.txt
grep -v -- "-----" cert.pem    | tr -d '\n' > cert_b64.txt

On Windows PowerShell, use the equivalent Get-Content, Where-Object and Set-Content commands. The public certificate goes to SuccessFactors and to the Postman variable certificate_b64. The private key goes only into the Postman variable private_key_b64, and it must never be shared.

Step C: Register the OAuth client in SuccessFactors

In Admin Center, open Manage OAuth2 Client Applications and choose Register Client Application. Fill in:

  • Company: the tenant company ID (prefilled).
  • Application Name: free text. It appears in the token as issuedFor.
  • Application URL: used for identification only. No call is made to it.
  • Bind to Users: checked, and the technical user ID added. This restricts token issuance to the listed users and is recommended.
  • X.509 Certificate: paste the single-line Base64 certificate.

Do not click Generate X.509 Certificate. That creates a different key pair, and you already have yours. After registering, open the client and copy the API Key. It becomes the Postman variable client_id. The API Key is not a secret on its own, but it cannot be used to obtain tokens without the private key.

Step Postman environment

Create an environment, for example SF ACME Preview, with these variables:

Variable Content

urlThe API server of your data center, without a trailing slash. This is not the UI URL. Find it in SAP's list of SuccessFactors API servers.
userThe technical user ID from Step A. It goes into the assertion NameID.
companyThe tenant company ID.
client_idThe API Key of the OAuth client.
private_key_b64Content of private_b64.txt. Set the type to secret and fill only the Current value.
certificate_b64Content of cert_b64.txt. Optional, added to the assertion KeyInfo.
assertion, assertion_xml, sf_token, sf_token_exp, sessionIdLeft empty. They are written by the requests.

Postman keeps an Initial value and a Current value for each variable. Keep the private key, tokens and assertions in the Current value only, so they are not synced to the workspace or included in exports.

Collection structure

The collection can be run from top to bottom with the Collection Runner, or one request at a time:

  • SF SAML Bearer step by step
    1. Generate assertion: downloads the jsrsasign library and builds the signed assertion.
    2. Get token: exchanges the assertion for an access token.
    3. Call OData resource: calls the OData API with the Bearer token.
  • CompoundEmployee
    • Login CE: opens the SFAPI session.
    • GET CompoundEmployee: runs the SOAP query.
  • AllInOneCall (optional): a pre-request script that obtains a token automatically when needed.

Request 1: Generating the SAML assertion

SuccessFactors does not create the assertion for you. The old /oauth/idp endpoint is deprecated, because it required sending the private key over the network. So the assertion has to be built and signed on the client side. Postman's sandbox includes CryptoJS for hashing but no RSA signing, so the script first downloads jsrsasign, a pure JavaScript cryptography library.

The assertion contains:

  • ID and IssueInstant: a random identifier and the current UTC time.
  • Issuer: the fixed value www.successfactors.com.
  • Signature: an enveloped XML signature, placed right after the Issuer.
  • Subject / NameID: the technical user the API calls will run as.
  • SubjectConfirmationData: the Recipient is the /oauth/token endpoint.
  • Conditions: a validity window from 5 minutes in the past to 10 minutes in the future.
  • AttributeStatement: an api_key attribute with the client ID, which tells SuccessFactors which registered certificate to use.

The signature is produced in three steps. First, the assertion without the signature is hashed with SHA-256. Second, a small SignedInfo block describing the algorithms and the digest is assembled. Third, SignedInfo is signed with the private key using RSA-SHA256. SuccessFactors repeats the same computation with the registered certificate. If one byte differs, the verification fails.

One detail matters a lot: XML signatures are computed over a canonical form of the XML (Exclusive XML Canonicalization, exc-c14n). Postman has no canonicalization library, so the script writes the XML already in canonical form, with no spaces or line breaks between elements, attributes in alphabetical order and explicit closing tags. Do not reformat or indent the XML parts of the script. A single extra space breaks the signature.

Request 2: Getting the access token

The assertion is exchanged at {{url}}/oauth/token as an x-www-form-urlencoded body with four fields: client_id, company_id, grant_type set to urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:saml2-bearer, and assertion. This must happen within the 10-minute window of the assertion.

The post-response script stores sf_token and an expiry timestamp. The expiry is set 5 minutes early to avoid using a token that expires in the middle of a call.

The token is Base64-encoded JSON. Decoding it is a useful sanity check, because it shows which API key and which user it was issued for.

Request 3: Calling the OData API

With the token, OData calls are simple: the token goes in the Authorization: Bearer header. For example:

  • GET {{url}}/odata/v2/User?$top=5&$format=json
  • GET {{url}}/odata/v2/PerPerson?$top=5&$format=json
  • GET {{url}}/odata/v2/EmpJob?$filter=userId eq '100001'&$select=userId,startDate,company,department,jobCode&$format=json

To check whether a token is still valid, call {{url}}/oauth/validate with the Bearer token.

CompoundEmployee via SFAPI

CompoundEmployee is exposed by the SFAPI, the older SOAP API. Unlike OData, SFAPI works with sessions. A login operation returns a session ID, which is also set as the JSESSIONID cookie, and every query must carry that session.

The key finding from testing: sending the Bearer token directly on the query returns INVALID_SESSION. The token must first be used in a login call, and the login body must have empty companyId, username and password elements. If companyId or username are filled in, SuccessFactors attempts a classic password login and fails with FAILED_AUTHENTICATION. If the password element is removed altogether, the request fails schema validation. So the working combination is empty elements plus the Bearer header, which returns a session ID.

Then, for the query:

  • Set the cookie explicitly: Cookie: JSESSIONID={{sessionId}}.
  • Disable the Postman cookie jar, so that old session cookies are not sent.
  • Use a SOAP query with a SELECT on CompoundEmployee, for example on person, personal_information, employment_information and job_information.
  • For incremental extracts, add a delta filter such as WHERE last_modified_on > to_datetime('...'). Inside XML, the greater-than sign must be written as >.
  • When the response contains <hasMore>true</hasMore>, call queryMore with the returned querySessionId until hasMore is false.

The SFAPI session expires after 10 minutes of inactivity. If you get INVALID_SESSION, run the login again.

Lifetimes and run order

Item Lifetime When to regenerate

SAML assertion10 minutesRun Request 1 again if Request 2 is sent later than that.
Access tokenAbout 24 hoursRun Requests 1 and 2 again. The step-by-step flow does not refresh automatically.
SFAPI session10 minutes of inactivityRun Login CE again on INVALID_SESSION.
CertificateAs generated, or as agreed with the customerRotate before expiry: new key pair, then update the OAuth client and the Postman variables together.

A typical session is: generate the assertion, get the token, call OData as needed, log in to SFAPI, then run the CompoundEmployee query.

Troubleshooting

A few of the errors encountered while building this setup:

  • Identifier 't' has already been declared: the library was loaded in the same scope as the script. Load it with new Function(...), as the script does.
  • getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND undefined: a variable does not exist in the selected environment. Check the variable names and that the environment is selected.
  • Error from KEYUTIL.getKey: the key is not PKCS#8 or it is truncated. Regenerate it with -nodes, and check that the first line is -----BEGIN PRIVATE KEY-----.
  • /oauth/token rejects the assertion: the certificate registered in SuccessFactors does not match the key, the XML was altered, the clocks are out of sync, or the assertion is older than 10 minutes.
  • INVALID_SESSION on SOAP calls: the query was sent with the Bearer token instead of the session cookie, or an old cookie was sent. Log in first and disable the cookie jar.
  • FAILED_AUTHENTICATION on login: the credential elements were not empty, or the Bearer header was not set on the request.

Security

  • The private key is equivalent to the credentials of the technical user. Keep it only in the Postman Current value, marked as secret. Never commit it to a repository or share it in chats. Ideally, each colleague generates their own key pair and OAuth client.
  • Never send tokens to third-party hosts. The request that downloads the library from cdnjs must use No Auth. An inherited Bearer token would be sent to that host.
  • Use a dedicated technical user with minimal permissions and a restricted target population, and enable Bind to Users on the OAuth client.
  • Use separate key pairs and OAuth clients for each tenant, for example preview and production.
  • Once OAuth works, remove the Basic Authentication permission from the technical user.

Attached material

The attached Postman collection, OAuth Assertion - SuccessFactors, contains all the requests described above, in the order they should run, the complete Request 1 script, and the optional AllInOneCall request, which handles token renewal automatically.

Note: SAP Community does not accept .json attachments, so the collection is provided as a .txt file. Rename it to OAuth_Assertion_SuccessFactors.postman_collection.json before importing it into Postman. The file content is unchanged.

Before importing it, create the environment described in Step D. The collection contains no secrets. All tenant data in the examples (URLs, company ID, user, API key, keys and IDs) are fictitious, so replace them with your own tenant values.

I hope this helps anyone who needs to test SuccessFactors APIs from Postman without Basic Authentication. Questions and feedback are welcome in the comments

entry.title: ONB 2.0: Recruiter-Based Task Assignment
entry.content:
SAP SuccessFactors Onboarding 2.0: Assigning the Recruiter from Recruiting as the Responsible User for Review New Hire Data and Onboarding Tasks

A business requirement that SAP does not support through its standard direct assignment scenario was addressed with a custom solution combining existing configuration components. In this article, I describe the implementation that assigns the Recruiter specified on the Job Requisition in Recruiting as the responsible user for both the Review New Hire Data step and Onboarding tasks.

SAP KBA 3550964 (Mapping roles in the JobRelType to New Hire Data Review Step assignee) and KBA 3599479 (Is it possible to delegate New Hire Data Review Task to someone else?) are the references we consulted regarding standard product behavior in this area. The method described here is not a standard feature published by SAP; it is a custom configuration developed as part of a project and must be validated in the relevant environment.

Important prerequisite: This solution relies on resolving the Employee HR role through the HR Manager relationship in Job Relationships. If the HR Manager relationship is used to represent a different person in the organization, this design may alter the existing relationship, route tasks to the wrong person, and may not be suitable. Check the existing use of Job Relationships before implementation.

The method consists of two parallel assignment paths: For Review New Hire Data, the Recruiter information is transferred to a custom employmentInfo field, and the responsible group is determined through ONB2ResponsibilityConfig. For other Onboarding tasks, an HR Manager relationship is created through Job Relationships mapping; the Employee HR role in the general HRBP Responsible Group resolves the relevant user based on that relationship.

Job Requisition Field and Save Rule

First, create a custom picklist field for Job Relationship Type in the Job Requisition Template. Its ID can be custJobRelType. This field must use the standard jobRelType picklist. Verify that Manage Business Configuration → Job Relationship → Job Relationship Type is configured with the same picklist. Since the field is used for background mapping, it does not have to be visible to end users.

 

<field-definition id="custJobRelType" type="picklist" required="false" custom="true">
  <field-label><![CDATA[Job Relationship Type]]></field-label>
  <field-label lang="en_US"><![CDATA[Job Relationship Type]]></field-label>
  <field-description><![CDATA[]]></field-description>
  <picklist-id>jobRelType</picklist-id>
</field-definition>

 XML: custJobRelType field definition for the Job Requisition Template

In Admin Center → Manage Rules in Recruiting, open the Job Requisition tab and select the template in use. Then, under Configure Business Rules, create a rule using the “Configure Business Rules on Job Requisition” scenario with Purpose = Save. IF = Always True; THEN = Job Requisition Template.Job Relationship Type = HR Manager.

Manage Rules in Recruiting: selecting an active Job Requisition Template

Save Rule: setting Job Relationship Type to HR Manager

Assign the rule to the Save section of all relevant Job Requisition Templates in use. This automatically populates the relationship type when the requisition is saved.

Recruit-to-Hire Data Mapping for Job Relationships

In Admin Center → Recruit-to-Hire Data Mapping → Job Relationships, create new mapping rows. In the implemented design, Relationship Type is sourced from the custom Job Relationship Type field on the Job Requisition; the related user is sourced from Recruiter (recruiterName); and the relationship start date is sourced from Start Date. Check the corresponding technical fields for these three mappings in your own template.

Recruit-to-Hire Data Mapping: Job Relationships mappings

Employment Information Field and Review New Hire Data Assignment

Under Admin Center → Manage Business Configuration → employmentInfo, configure an available custom String field. The example below uses custom-string24; a different custom string field can also be selected.

Manage Business Configuration: employmentInfo object

Field settings:

  • Identifier = custom-string24;
  • Label = HRBP (ONB);
  • Enabled = Yes;
  • Mandatory = No;
  • Data Type = STRING;
  • Type of Reference Object = Foundation Object;
  • Reference Object = ONB2ResponsibilityConfig;
  • Maximum Length = 256.

As this field is intended for background use, it does not need to be displayed on the candidate screen.

Next, under Recruit-to-Hire Data Mapping → Employment Information (employmentInfo), map custom-string24 to the source Job Requisition Template → Recruiter (recruiterName). This transfers the Recruiter information to the field used by the Review New Hire Data responsibility rule.

Employment Information: mapping custom-string24 to Recruiter

In Configure Business Rules, configure the SFCC_ResponsibleForNewHireDataReview rule using the “Assign Responsibility Group for New Hire Data Review” scenario. The rule selects the relevant Responsible Group from the employmentInfo field referencing ONB2ResponsibilityConfig. The Responsible Group ID created for each Recruiter must match the technical value resolved from this field. Verify the exact IF/THEN expression against the environment configuration shown in the screenshot below.

SFCC_ResponsibleForNewHireDataReview: rule determining the Responsible Group

Responsible Groups:

In Admin Center → Onboarding General Settings → Manage Responsible Groups, first create the general HRBP group. ID = HRBP, Group Name = HRBP, Roles = Employee HR. Leave Users and Dynamic Groups empty. This general group will be assigned to Onboarding tasks in the program.

General HRBP Responsible Group: Employee HR role

On the same screen, create a separate, user-specific Responsible Group for each Recruiter/HRBP. The Group ID and name must match the relevant employee ID; add only the corresponding employee to Users; leave Roles and Dynamic Groups empty. The value 642317 in the example is illustrative. These are the groups identified by the Review New Hire Data rule.

User-specific Responsible Group: employee ID and user

This distinction is critical: Review New Hire Data identifies the user-specific group ID through the custom field and rule. Other tasks in the Onboarding program are assigned to the general HRBP group; the Employee HR role in this group resolves to the user designated as HR Manager through Job Relationships mapping.

Task Assignment in the Onboarding Program

In Admin Center → Manage Onboarding and Offboarding Programs, open the relevant program. Edit the task to be routed under Primary New Hire Tasks or Secondary New Hire Tasks. Select Task Attributes → Assigned to = HRBP. The same setting was used for the Equipment task, for example. Repeat this assignment for other relevant tasks.

Onboarding Program: Task Attributes → Assigned to = HRBP

Conclusion and Considerations

In this custom solution, the Recruiter information serves two separate mechanisms. For Review New Hire Data, a user-specific group is selected using an ONB2ResponsibilityConfig Lookup. For Onboarding tasks, an HR Manager relationship is created through Job Relationships, and the assignment is made to the general HRBP group using the Employee HR role. Thus, instead of a direct Recruiter → Task Assignee mapping, existing responsibility and relationship mechanisms are combined.

Before go-live, test each candidate to confirm that the Recruiter user ID resolves correctly, the Job Relationship is created with the correct person and start date, the user-specific Responsible Group ID matches its value, and both task types are assigned to the correct user. If the HR Manager relationship is used in other processes, this method should not be implemented, or the design should be reassessed.

Note: If dashboard visibility is separated based on Granted Users / Target Population permissions after this structure is configured, each Recruiter will see only their own candidates on the dashboard. However, because the configuration steps for this adjustment are not included in the document, this blog technically explains only the task assignee solution; it does not cover the separation of dashboard visibility.

entry.title: Managing Inactive Contacts in Email Marketing: Balancing Deliverability Risk with List Value
entry.content:
Why Inactive Contacts Carry Both Value and Risk

Inactive contacts — subscribers on a mailing list who have not recently opened, clicked, or converted — are a normal part of every email marketing programme. They carry both value and risk.

The value: sending to inactive contacts performs a discovery function, identifying contacts who are naturally returning to a buying phase. Excluding them entirely makes it harder to build brand awareness, retain customers, and identify signals that indicate where a contact is in the customer lifecycle.

The risk: mismanaging inactive contacts — sending too frequently, sending irrelevant content, or failing to remove contacts who have been inactive for too long — damages sender reputation and causes deliverability issues, including blocked emails, bounced messages, and loss of inbox placement.

The goal is not to eliminate inactive contacts from the programme but to manage them in a way that captures their value while controlling the risk they introduce. This article explains both how to measure the health of that balance using proactive metrics, and how to act on those metrics through data management and targeting strategy.

Why Inactive Contacts Are a Normal and Valuable Part of Email Marketing

After a full-list send — an email sent to the entire mailing list rather than a targeted segment — the majority of opens, clicks, and conversions will come from the most active contacts. This is expected. However, a proportion of engagement and revenue will also come from contacts who were classified as inactive before that campaign.

This happens because sending to the full list performs a discovery function: it identifies contacts who are naturally returning to an active buying phase. This is why even unsegmented email programmes — sometimes called batch-and-blast sending, where the same email is sent to the entire list without segmentation — produce results.

Discovery marketing can be thought of as the complement to targeting. Where targeting delivers content based on what is already known about a contact's behaviour and preferences, discovery marketing involves sending broader content to uncover new areas of interest and to identify contacts who are becoming active again.

Every successful email marketing programme has a combination of active and inactive contacts. The goal is not to remove inactive contacts entirely, but to manage them in a way that captures their value while controlling the deliverability risk they introduce.

How Inactive Contact Data Causes Deliverability Issues

If an established email marketing programme experiences deliverability issues — blocked or bounced emails, or messages going to the junk folder instead of the inbox — the cause is almost always related to the data being sent to.

Email filters operated by mailbox providers (such as Gmail, Microsoft/Outlook, and Yahoo) are designed to deliver emails that recipients find valuable, and to block, suppress, or hide emails that are unwanted. When a sender's domain authentication and email content are consistent and properly configured, a deliverability problem almost always points to the data. In our support case experience, data issues typically fall into one or more of three categories:

  1. Invalid data that should not have been added to the list. This includes mistyped addresses, fake addresses, and bot-generated sign-ups that were not caught by validation at the point of sign-up. For guidance on preventing invalid data from entering a list, see the companion article: Clean Start Validation: How to Prevent Poor-Quality Email Addresses Entering Your List at Sign-Up.
  2. Campaign engagement rate — the ratio of active to inactive contacts in each send. Sending a high volume of email to contacts who do not engage signals to mailbox providers that the content is unwanted, reducing sender reputation over time.
  3. Long-term inactive data that should have been removed. Contacts who have been on the list for an extended period without engaging may include spam traps — email addresses operated by mailbox providers and anti-spam organisations to identify senders with poor list hygiene — and other high-risk addresses that actively damage sender reputation.

When a deliverability issue is suspected, sender authentication and email content should always be tested as part of any investigation. However, in practice, data issues are the most common root cause.

Why Traditional Deliverability Reporting Alone Does Not Prevent Problems

Standard deliverability reporting — covering metrics such as bounce rate, spam complaint rate, domain reputation scores, and inbox placement rate — is diagnostic in nature. It identifies what went wrong and where, but only after the problem has already occurred.

While diagnostic reporting is valuable for understanding past performance and identifying trends, it is inherently reactive. Relying solely on these metrics to guide an email programme leads to a repeating cycle: an issue is detected, a fix is applied, the same or a similar issue recurs, because the underlying cause — typically a data management or targeting problem — has not been addressed.

To break this cycle, email marketers need metrics that monitor the ongoing health and risk factors of the email programme, highlighting where problems are developing before they result in deliverability failures. The following section describes the proactive health metrics I recommend for identifying these risks early.

Proactive Health and Risk Metrics for Email Programmes

I recommend the following metrics for monitoring the health of an email programme proactively. They are designed to highlight risks in data quality, targeting, and list management before those risks cause deliverability problems.

Percentage of Active Compared to Inactive Contacts

What proportion of the mailing list is actively engaging with emails? A declining active percentage over time indicates that list growth is not keeping pace with disengagement, or that re-engagement efforts are insufficient. Monitoring this metric monthly provides an early warning of list health decline.

Monthly Email Volume to Active Compared to Inactive Contacts

How many emails are sent each month to active contacts compared to inactive contacts? This metric reveals how much of the programme's volume is driven by targeted, engagement-based sending compared to broad or untargeted campaigns. A high proportion of volume going to inactive contacts indicates that targeting and automation should be reviewed.

Active Message Volume Percentage

What share of total monthly email volume is sent to active recipients? I recommend a target of 50% or higher, which generally indicates strong list quality and effective targeting. Below this threshold, the programme may be over-relying on inactive contacts to generate volume, which increases deliverability risk.

Inactive Contact Segmentation: Previous Customers Compared to Unengaged Addresses

Among inactive contacts, what proportion are previous customers with a proven purchase or engagement history, compared to contacts who have never meaningfully engaged — sometimes called "zombie" addresses? This distinction matters because previous customers have demonstrated value and may re-engage, while contacts who have never engaged are more likely to be invalid, temporary, or bot-generated. This metric helps assess both list quality and the effectiveness of data lifecycle management.

New Subscriber Engagement Rate

What percentage of new subscribers engage with emails within their first weeks on the list? A low new-subscriber engagement rate may indicate problems with sign-up validation, the effectiveness of the welcome programme, or the quality of the traffic source driving sign-ups. In our experience, approximately 5–10% of new sign-ups remaining completely inactive is a normal baseline. Above 10%, the sign-up process and traffic sources should be investigated.

How to Balance Active and Inactive Contact Management

Managing inactive contacts effectively requires balancing send frequency, content strategy, and re-engagement processes. I recommend the following approaches.

Reduce Send Frequency for Inactive Contacts

Send emails to inactive contacts less often than to active contacts. A practical target is to balance the total monthly email volume so that the number of emails sent to active contacts is equal to or greater than the number sent to inactive contacts.

Most established mailing lists have more inactive contacts than active. This natural imbalance provides a useful frequency guideline. For example, if a mailing list has three times more inactive contacts than active, active contacts should receive approximately three times more emails per month to achieve an even volume balance across the programme.

Use Different Content for Inactive Contacts

Sales-focused content can alienate even loyal customers if they are not in a buying phase, and repeated sales emails to disengaged contacts can train recipients to ignore or filter out future messages. Instead of sales content, email content aligned with blog articles, social media content, educational material, or brand storytelling gives inactive contacts a reason to open, read, and click through to the website — strengthening brand awareness and retention without requiring an immediate purchase.

Introduce Re-Engagement Automation for Returning Contacts

For programmes that use separate content streams for active and inactive contacts, a re-engagement automation sequence — a series of automated emails, similar in structure to a welcome campaign, designed to gradually rebuild engagement — can be introduced for contacts who begin interacting again. This sequence transitions returning contacts back into the main sending programme gradually, rather than immediately placing them back into the full sales email cycle.

How to Recover When Deliverability Issues Occur

If deliverability issues arise — including bounced or blocked emails, or loss of inbox placement — recovery is achievable. The process involves two parallel workstreams: an immediate reputation rebuild using active data, and a longer-term rebalancing of the sending programme to address the underlying cause.

Immediate Steps to Rebuild Sender Reputation

  • Send to active data only. Temporarily restrict sending to new sign-ups and the most engaged contacts. This demonstrates to mailbox providers (such as Gmail, Microsoft/Outlook, and Yahoo) that recipients value the emails, which rebuilds sender reputation and restores inbox placement. In practice, minor issues can recover in a matter of days, while more serious issues may take two to four weeks.
  • Check sign-up processes. Send to new contacts and active contacts in separate campaigns to clearly identify the bounce and engagement rates of new data. New sign-ups should have low bounce rates and high engagement. If they do not, sign-up forms and validation processes should be reviewed to ensure new data is valid and being collected correctly.

Rebalancing the Programme While Reputation Recovers

While the reputation rebuild is underway, use the time to address the underlying causes that led to the issue:

  • Remove the oldest, least-active data. Identify the oldest contacts who have shown no meaningful engagement — particularly those who have been on the list for years without ever clicking a link or visiting the website. This segment is likely to contain spam traps — email addresses operated by mailbox providers and anti-spam organisations to identify senders with poor list hygiene — and other high-risk addresses.
  • Review inactive send frequency. Adjust segments and automation programmes to reduce the weekly and monthly frequency of emails to inactive contacts. When reviewing monthly totals, the target should be for the total volume of emails sent to active contacts to exceed the volume sent to inactive contacts.
  • Review content for inactive contacts. Long-term inactivity is a signal that the content being sent is not what those contacts want. Introduce a different content approach — educational content, brand content, or other material that gives contacts a new reason to open, read, and click through.
  • Restart gradually. Once deliverability has recovered, reintroduce email marketing to inactive contacts with improved data quality, adjusted content strategy, and reduced frequency. Increase volume gradually and monitor the proactive health metrics described in this article to ensure the programme remains balanced.

Summary: Proactive Monitoring and Informed Strategy Work Together

Inactive contacts are a normal and valuable part of every email marketing programme. They generate revenue, support brand awareness, and help identify contacts returning to an active buying phase. However, mismanaging them — through excessive send frequency, irrelevant content, or failure to remove long-term inactive data — is the most common cause of email deliverability problems.

The key principles are:

  • Inactive contacts are normal and should not be excluded entirely. Every successful email programme includes a mix of active and inactive contacts. The goal is to manage the balance, not eliminate one side.
  • Deliverability issues are almost always caused by data problems. Invalid data, poor engagement ratios, and long-term inactive contacts are the most common root causes when authentication and content are already in order.
  • Reactive reporting diagnoses problems but does not prevent them. Traditional deliverability metrics identify issues after they occur. Proactive health metrics — active contact percentage, volume balance, inactive segmentation, and new subscriber engagement — identify risks before they cause failures.
  • Strategy must follow measurement. Health metrics show where the risks are. Strategic actions — validating new data, balancing send frequency, adjusting content for inactive contacts, and managing the data lifecycle — address them.
  • Recovery is possible. When deliverability issues occur, rebuilding sender reputation with active data while rebalancing frequency, content, and data quality resolves the underlying cause and helps prevent recurrence.

Neither measurement nor strategy alone is sufficient. Proactive health monitoring identifies emerging risks; informed data management and targeting decisions address them. Together, they build a sustainable email programme that captures the value of inactive contacts while controlling the deliverability risk they introduce.

1. Prerequisites to Validate Before Setting WBS to CLSD

Before changing the WBS/AFE to CLSD, validate:

Project System (PS)

WBS status is TECO (or equivalent project completion status).
No open networks, activities, milestones, or subordinate WBS elements.
No open reservations assigned to project activities.
No open project stock.

MM / Procurement

No open PRs.
No open POs.
No pending Goods Receipts (GRs).
No pending Invoice Receipts (IRs).
No remaining commitments.

FI / CO

All actual costs posted.
Period-end settlement executed successfully.
Settlement balances cleared.
AuC capitalization completed (if applicable).
No balance remaining on the WBS.
Budget checks completed (if budget-controlled project).


Recommended Transactions

CJ20N – Project Builder
CJ03 – Display WBS
CJI3 – Actual Cost Line Items
CJI5 – Commitments
S_ALR_87013558 – Cost Elements: Actual/Commitment/Total
CJ88 – Settlement
AIBU/ABJON/AUC reports (depending on asset process)

2. Reports for Key Closure Checks

3. PO Deleted or Fully Consumed but Commitment Appears in CJI5

Before concluding it is a commitment inconsistency, verify:

ME23N

Is PO item really deleted?
Is Final Delivery indicator set?
Is Final Invoice indicator set?

ME2N

Check open quantity/value.

ME5A

Verify whether the originating PR still exists.

CJI5

Review commitment category:
PR commitment
PO commitment
Reservation commitment

Run commitment rebuild/recalculation checks only after confirming source documents are no longer valid.

In many cases, the commitment comes from a remaining PR or partially open purchasing document rather than a true inconsistency.

4. PO Deleted but PR Commitment Remains

This is usually standard behavior if the PR remains active.

Recommended process:

Display PR in ME53N.
Determine whether PR is still required.
If not required:
Delete PR item, or
Set final deletion indicator.
Recheck commitment in CJI5 after update.

Only if:

PR is deleted,
PO is deleted,
and commitment still exists,

should you investigate a potential inconsistency.

entry.title: Configuring Process Parameters in SAP IPD Formulation
entry.content:
Introduction

SAP Integrated Product Development (SAP IPD) represents a transformative shift in how process industry organizations manage product formulations and manufacturing processes. At its core, the IPD framework with among others the Formulation solution provide product developers with a collaborative, integrated platform to manage recipes from initial concept through production. However, one of the more sophisticated features that elevates IPD beyond basic recipe management is the ability to configure and apply process parameters that precisely define how a recipe should be manufactured.

Want to see the full system demo? Check out the recording of our recent Product Expert Training session here (SAP Learning Hub license required).

Process parameters are the manufacturing conditions and constraints that ensure quality and consistency in product production. These parameters can include temperature ranges, processing times, mixing speeds, and pressure requirements - essentially any critical manufacturing condition that must be documented and controlled. This blog provides a comprehensive guide to configuring process parameters in SAP IPD, enabling administrators and product developers to implement production-ready recipe management systems.

Understanding Process Parameters

Process parameters describe the manufacturing conditions under which a recipe should be produced. Rather than simply listing ingredients and their quantities, process parameters allow recipe developers to specify the precise conditions required at each manufacturing stage. In a practical example such as producing apple soda, process parameters might dictate that the pasteurization step requires a specific temperature maintained for a defined duration, followed by mixing at a particular speed for a set time.

These parameters are not optional annotations but essential metadata that ensures regulatory compliance, maintains product quality, and enables effective knowledge transfer between teams and facilities. By embedding process parameters directly within recipe records, organizations create a single source of truth for how products should be manufactured, reducing variability and improving consistency across production sites.

[Image showing the configuration flow as outlined in the text.]

The Three-Step Configuration Framework

Configuring process parameters in SAP IPD follows a clearly defined workflow:

[Image showing steps 1-3 of the configuration flow as outlined in the text.]

Step 1: Property Configuration

The configuration journey begins in the IPD Specification Management’s Properties app, which serves as the template layer for specification attributes. Administrators create a new property specifically designated for Recipe Process Parameters, a special usage classification that signals this property will support manufacturing control parameters.

Within this property, administrators define the specific attributes that every process parameter should inherit. These attributes form the foundation for how process parameters can be used and maintained throughout the system. Common attribute fields include:

  • Value: The primary numeric value of the process parameter
  • Unit of Measure: Specifies whether the parameter is measured in minutes, degrees Celsius, RPM, etc.
  • Minimum and Maximum Values: Define acceptable ranges for the parameter
  • Operators: Allow specification of conditions such as "greater than," "less than," or "equal to"

[Image showing the Properties app with settings for unit of measure and currency]

Architectural insight: A single property configured with these attributes can serve as a template for multiple process parameters. This design principle ensures consistency while eliminating redundant configuration. If product needs evolve and additional attributes are required, administrators can either extend the existing property or create supplementary properties that link to specific process parameters.

Step 2: Data Synchronization

Once the property has been configured in the Properties app, administrators navigate to the Synchronize Data for Formulation" app to synchronize the data. This step ensures that the newly created property definition is propagated to the recipe formulation system, making it available for use when creating actual process parameters.

This explicit synchronization step, though seemingly administrative, serves an important purpose: it creates a clear audit trail and ensures that recipe developers always work with validated, consistent process parameter definitions. Without this synchronization, newly configured properties would remain invisible to the formulation environment.

Step 3: Process Parameter Creation

With data synchronized, administrators proceed to the primary configuration application: IPD Formulation’s Configure Process Parameters. Here, the actual process parameters that will be used in recipes are created and managed.

To create a new process parameter, administrators:

  1. Click on “Create” in the Configure Process Parameter app
  2. Enter the parameter's name and a unique identifier
  3. Optionally add descriptions and translations to support global organizations
  4. Critically, assign the previously configured property to this process parameter

[Image showing the Configure Process Parameters app with properties tab.]

Once the property is assigned, all attributes defined in that property become available in the process parameter automatically. Additionally, administrators can specify default values for minimum and maximum ranges, which will appear as baseline values when recipe developers add this parameter to their recipes.

Finally, administrators must change the process parameter's status from "In Work" to "Released," signaling that the parameter is validated and ready for use in recipe development.

From Configuration to Recipe Application

Once a process parameter reaches "Released" status, product developers gain access to it when creating or editing recipes. The process parameter appears as an available selection in the recipe's Process tab, which is specifically designed for documenting manufacturing stages and their associated conditions.

[Image showing the maintenance of process parameter values as outlined in the text.]

When a recipe developer adds a process parameter to a specific manufacturing stage, such as adding "Mixing Time" to the "Mixing" stage, the system automatically populates all attributes defined in the property. The developer can then:

  • Specify the target value for this manufacturing stage
  • Override default minimum and maximum values if stage-specific conditions differ
  • Select an appropriate unit of measure from the pre-configured options
  • Document any special operational instructions through operator fields

This workflow ensures that process parameters are consistently applied while allowing sufficient flexibility for stage-specific adjustments.

Key Benefits and Design Insights

Scalability and Consistency

The architecture of process parameters in SAP IPD demonstrates excellent scalability. By creating flexible property templates, organizations can define dozens of process parameters while maintaining consistency across all formulations. New parameters can be added without architectural changes or system redesign.

Knowledge Preservation

By formalizing process parameters in system records, organizations preserve institutional knowledge about manufacturing processes. When experienced operators move to different roles or retire, their manufacturing expertise remains documented and accessible to their successors.

Cross-Functional Collaboration

IPD's integration of process parameters with its collaborative environment enables engineering teams, quality assurance, and production teams to align on manufacturing requirements from the outset, reducing miscommunication and revision cycles.

Advanced Configuration Considerations

While the basic workflow is straightforward, administrators should consider several advanced aspects:

  • Allowed Units of Measure: Within property configuration, administrators can restrict the allowed units of measure for a parameter, simplifying user selection and preventing unit conversion errors.
  • Multiple Properties per parameter: While a single property can serve most needs, complex process parameters might require multiple properties. For example, a "Temperature Control" parameter might have one property for steady-state conditions and another for ramp-up specifications.
  • Translation and Localization: The property configuration interface supports multiple languages, enabling organizations with global operations to label parameters appropriately for regional teams.

Conclusion

Configuring process parameters in SAP IPD represents a maturation of recipe management from basic ingredient documentation to comprehensive manufacturing specification. By following the three-step configuration framework - defining property templates, synchronizing data, and creating released parameters - administrators can establish a robust foundation for consistent, auditable, and compliant recipe development.

SAP IPD process parameter functionality exemplifies how modern PLM systems serve not merely as data repositories but as active quality control instruments that embed manufacturing expertise directly into product development workflows.

entry.title: VSR Optimizer Why Its Real Input Isn't Data, It's Judgment
entry.content:
Ask a seasoned dispatcher how they build a day’s plan and you’ll get an answer that sounds like intuition this customer hates early deliveries, that lane always backs up after 3 PM, those two orders ride together because they always have. Ask the SAP TM Vehicle Scheduling and Routing (VSR) optimizer the same question and you get something unsettlingly honest I minimized a number. Tell me what the number should be. The most underappreciated feature in Transportation Management. Not the algorithm, but the question it forces you to answer.

How the VSR Optimizer Works:
The VSR optimizer takes a set of freight units (the demand side) and a set of vehicle resources, schedules and carriers (the supply side). It searches for an assignment: which shipments ride on which vehicles, in what sequence, departing when. The search space is astronomically large. Ten freight units across three trucks already produce more feasible plans than a human can. The optimizer navigates this space against constraints (vehicle capacities, opening hours, driving-time regulations, incompatibilities) and a total cost function, the thing a plan should minimize. Most of the costs in that function are not real.

Understanding Optimization Costs and Penalties:
The cost function blends actual freight charges with penalty costs you invent: a cost per vehicle deployed, a cost per kilometer, a cost per hour, and penalties for early delivery, late delivery and not planning a freight unit at all. None of these invoice anyone. They exist to encode your priorities in a language the algorithm understands.


Figure 1: Planning profile cost settings

Set the non delivery penalty low, and the optimizer will cheerfully leave inconvenient orders behind.
Set earliness and lateness penalties symmetric, and it treats a dock appointment like a suggestion.
Make the per vehicle fixed cost dominant, and it will contort routes to save one truck. This is the part implementation teams underestimate. The optimizer is not a settings screen you configure once; it is a mirror. If your plans come out wrong, the uncomfortable diagnosis is usually that the costs faithfully reflect what you said you value, not what you actually do.

Practical Example:
Freight Consolidation vs Delivery Performance Consider two orders to the same region one 900 kg parcel due Thursday, one 11-tonne load due Friday. A human planner ships them separately: two clean plans, two happy customers, two half-empty trucks. The optimizer, facing a vehicle fixed cost of 500 units against a lateness penalty of 10 per hour, does the arithmetic the planner never writes down. Holding the Thursday order one day and consolidating costs 240 in lateness penalties but saves 500 in vehicle cost. It merges them.

Figure 2: Optimization result with the two Atlanta orders consolidated on one vehicle

Considering Carbon Emissions in Transportation Planning, CO₂ can enter this same calculus. An internal carbon price stops being hypothetical the moment it becomes a cost term the optimizer minimizes alongside distance and duration.

Using VSR Optimization to Improve Transportation Decisions
Run it as a sparring partner, not an autocrat. Interactive planning in the Transportation Cockpit lets planners override the proposal, and the overrides are data. If humans consistently reverse the same category of decision, either train the planners or fix the costs.
Simulate before you commit. Because the cost function is just parameters, counterfactuals are cheap: cut the fleet by two vehicles, tighten delivery windows by four hours, or price carbon at €100 a tonne instead of €50. A profile copy and a re-run replace a consulting engagement.
Let it expose your constraints. Unplanned freight units are the optimizer’s way of filing a complaint. A pattern of unplannable demand on a lane is a procurement insight wearing an error message’s clothing.
Close the loop with execution. Feeding actual transit times back into planning parameters turns every executed freight order into a calibration point.

Conclusion
The SAP TM VSR optimizer demonstrates how transportation planning decisions are influenced not only by freight data and operational constraints but also by the cost parameters and penalties configured by the business. Through the freight consolidation example and practical planning scenarios discussed, we can see how appropriate cost settings, planner judgment, and continuous evaluation of optimization results can improve transportation efficiency and decision making. The key takeaway is that while the optimizer identifies the best solution based on configured objectives, transportation professionals must ensure those objectives reflect actual business priorities.

entry.title: BTP Transports with CTMS & Content Agent | Part 3: Second Content Agent and target in Central
entry.content:
Part 3 of the series BTP Transports with CTMS & Content Agent.

In Part 2 we set up Dev, so a parcel can now be packed and dropped at the source node. In this part we build the receiving end in Central: a second Content Agent that unpacks the parcel, the connection CTMS uses to reach it, and the connection it uses to write into the target Integration Suite.

 

Before you start

The target Integration Suite runs in Central, with the Cloud Integration capability activated (the same rule as in Dev).

Step 1: Process Integration Runtime instance and key

Same as in Dev: an instance of SAP Process Integration Runtime, plan api, with the roles WorkspacePackagesRead, WorkspacePackagesEdit and WorkspacePackagesTransport, and a service key. This time it gives the unpacker access to the target workspace.

Step 2: The second Content Agent

  • Create an instance of Content Agent service with the application plan and the role Import. This is the unpacker.
  • Create a service key. You need its url and, from the uaa section, clientid, clientsecret and url.

Step 3: CloudIntegration destination in Central

The unpacker writes into Integration Suite through a destination named CloudIntegration, filled exactly like the Dev one in Part 2, but from the key of step 1. You can also let the Content Agent UI create it for you when you activate the Cloud Integration content type (see "What tripped me up" first).

Step 4: The transport destination CTMS uses

CTMS needs to know where to deliver the parcel. In Central, create a destination for that. Its name is free; I used CAS_on_target.

FieldValue
URLurl from the Content Agent key (step 2)
AuthenticationOAuth2ClientCredentials
Client ID / secretclientid / clientsecret from the uaa section
Token Service URLurl from the uaa section + /oauth/token

Step 5: Finish the target node

Open CTMS, edit the target node from Part 1 and pick CAS_on_target as its destination. The content type stays Multi-Target Application.

 

The target node with its content type and destination.

A green Check Connection on CAS_on_target only proves the address is reachable (Part 2 explains why). The real test is the first transport in Part 4.

What tripped me up in my setup

  • Three identical runtime instances. Central had three Process Integration Runtime instances with the same name, each in a different Cloud Foundry space, left over from earlier attempts. Before copying a key I had to check which space the target Cloud Integration actually runs in, and use the instance from that space. Clear names would have saved me this.
  • Activating the content type failed because the destination already existed. Activating the Cloud Integration content type in the Content Agent UI creates a CloudIntegration destination for you. I had already created one by hand, so the activation did not go through. It also asks for a Cloud Foundry passcode, and I first suspected the login URL and changed it to the Cloud Foundry API endpoint, which changed nothing. The fix was simple: I edited my existing CloudIntegration destination, added the client secret, and the activation went through. Either create the destination by hand or let the Content Agent UI do it, not both.

Roles for this part

Instance roles only: the three Workspace roles on the runtime instance and Import on the Content Agent instance. The user roles come in Part 4, and Part 7 lists them all.

What comes next

Both ends are now connected. In Part 4 we switch on Transport in Integration Suite, send the first package and import it in CTMS, including the role that kept the Transport option greyed out for me.
